q: Following a road traffic accident with blunt chest trauma, a 30-year-old man has a tube thoracostomy placed that drains 1600 mL of blood immediately upon insertion, and he remains tachycardic and hypotensive despite fluid resuscitation. Which of the following best determines the need for emergency thoracotomy in this patient?
opts: Any hemothorax requiring a chest tube for drainage
Persistent chest pain after chest tube insertion
Initial drainage >1500 mL of blood, or ongoing drainage >200 mL/hour for 2-4 consecutive hours
Hemothorax visible on chest X-ray without hemodynamic instability
why: Most traumatic hemothoraces are managed with a chest tube alone; it is the volume/rate that defines the massive subset needing surgery
Pain alone, without volume criteria or instability, is not a surgical indication
Correct — standard volume/rate criteria for emergency thoracotomy in massive hemothorax
Imaging alone, without defined output or instability, does not mandate surgery
exp: Massive hemothorax is a volume/rate diagnosis, not just any hemothorax on imaging: initial drainage >1500 mL or sustained >200 mL/hr for 2-4h signals a major vascular injury a chest tube alone won't control, and is the trigger for thoracotomy.

q: A 35-year-old woman with untreated Graves' disease undergoes emergency appendectomy. Twelve hours postoperatively she develops a temperature of 39.5C, heart rate of 160/min, agitation, and altered sensorium, a presumed thyroid storm. Which sequence of pharmacological management is most appropriate?
opts: Start Lugol's iodine first, followed by propylthiouracil
Give a beta-blocker and propylthiouracil (or methimazole) first, then Lugol's iodine at least an hour later, followed by hydrocortisone
Give a beta-blocker alone and observe for 24 hours
why: Giving iodine before the thionamide can hand the gland fresh substrate and worsen the crisis
Correct sequence for thyroid storm management
Radioactive iodine has far too slow an onset to help in an acute crisis
Beta-blockade alone does not stop ongoing hormone synthesis/release in a life-threatening storm
exp: In thyroid storm the sequence matters: beta-blocker plus thionamide first, iodine at least an hour later (never before the thionamide, or it fuels new hormone synthesis), then stress-dose steroids, which also block peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion.

q: A 48-year-old woman undergoes modified radical mastectomy for breast cancer and desires reconstruction. She has a thin body habitus with inadequate abdominal donor tissue for a free flap. Which pedicled flap, based on the thoracodorsal vessels, is most suitable?
opts: Transverse rectus abdominis myocutaneous (TRAM) free flap
why: Correct: thoracodorsal-pedicled flap that does not need abdominal donor tissue
DIEP requires adequate lower abdominal tissue, which this patient lacks
TRAM also needs abdominal donor tissue and adds microsurgical risk
Gracilis is a thigh-based free flap, not the standard first choice here
exp: When abdominal donor tissue is inadequate for a DIEP or TRAM flap, the latissimus dorsi myocutaneous flap, pedicled on the thoracodorsal vessels, remains a reliable pedicled (non-microsurgical) reconstructive option.

q: A 24-year-old man sustains a head injury in a fall and presents with periorbital ecchymosis, bruising over the mastoid process, and clear fluid dripping from the nose that leaves a double-ring (halo) stain on gauze. He is conscious and oriented. What is the most appropriate initial management?
opts: Immediate surgical repair of the dural defect
Insertion of a nasogastric tube to confirm CSF rhinorrhea
Anterior nasal packing to stop the fluid leak
Conservative management: head elevation, avoiding nose-blowing, and monitoring for meningitis, since most leaks resolve spontaneously within days
why: Surgery is reserved for leaks persisting beyond about 1-2 weeks or with complications, not the initial step
An NG tube is contraindicated in suspected basal skull fracture due to risk of intracranial passage
Packing does not treat the underlying dural tear and raises infection risk
Correct: most basal skull fracture CSF leaks seal spontaneously with conservative care
exp: Basilar skull fracture with CSF rhinorrhea (halo/ring sign on gauze, raccoon eyes, Battle's sign) is managed conservatively first; the majority seal within 7-10 days, and a nasogastric tube must be avoided given the risk of intracranial passage through the fracture.

q: A 60-year-old man presents with a 12-hour history of a previously reducible right inguinal swelling that has become irreducible, tender, and erythematous, with vomiting and absolute constipation. He is tachycardic with a mild fever. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
opts: Attempt manual taxis (reduction) under sedation and observe
Emergency surgical exploration without delay, since findings suggest strangulation
Elective herniorrhaphy after resolving obstruction with nasogastric decompression
Ultrasound-guided reduction followed by outpatient follow-up
why: Forceful taxis in a strangulated hernia risks reducing non-viable bowel into the abdomen, masking ongoing sepsis
Correct: erythema, tenderness, and systemic toxicity with irreducibility indicate strangulation, a surgical emergency
Delay risks bowel perforation and peritonitis
Not appropriate once signs of strangulation are present
exp: Irreducibility plus erythema, tenderness, and systemic toxicity in a hernia signals strangulated bowel and is a surgical emergency; forceful taxis is dangerous here because non-viable bowel can be reduced en masse, hiding ongoing sepsis until the patient deteriorates.

q: A 32-year-old man undergoes radical inguinal orchidectomy for a testicular mass; histopathology confirms pure seminoma confined to the testis, with normal postoperative tumor markers. Which statement best describes management specific to seminoma compared to non-seminomatous germ cell tumors (NSGCT)?
opts: Seminoma requires primary bleomycin-based chemotherapy regardless of stage
Seminoma is managed identically to NSGCT, with retroperitoneal lymph node dissection (RPLND) as standard
Seminoma is highly radiosensitive; surveillance or adjuvant radiotherapy/chemotherapy to para-aortic nodes is preferred over RPLND
Seminoma has the worst prognosis among germ cell tumors and needs aggressive upfront multimodal therapy
why: Chemotherapy is reserved for higher-stage or bulky disease, not routine low-stage seminoma
RPLND is more the NSGCT-favoured surgical approach, not seminoma's
Correct: seminoma's radiosensitivity is why surveillance/radiotherapy is favoured over RPLND
Seminoma actually carries a better prognosis than most NSGCT subtypes
exp: Pure seminoma is exquisitely radiosensitive and chemosensitive, which is exactly why low-stage disease is managed with surveillance or adjuvant radiotherapy/single-agent carboplatin rather than retroperitoneal lymph node dissection, the pathway more associated with NSGCT.

q: A 58-year-old chronic smoker presents with progressive facial puffiness, distended neck and upper chest veins, and headache worsened on bending forward. Examination shows non-pulsatile jugular venous distension not reducing with inspiration. Contrast CT chest reveals a right paratracheal mass compressing a major mediastinal vessel. Which vessel is most likely obstructed?
why: Correct: classic SVC syndrome from bronchogenic carcinoma compression
PA obstruction causes pulmonary hypertension/right heart strain, not this facial venous congestion pattern
Isolated azygos obstruction does not produce this syndrome
Aortic compression does not cause venous congestion
exp: Facial and upper-limb edema with non-pulsatile, non-collapsing neck vein distension and dilated chest wall collaterals in a smoker with a paratracheal mass is classic superior vena cava syndrome, most commonly from bronchogenic carcinoma compressing or invading the SVC.

q: A 45-year-old woman presents with rapid-onset breast erythema, warmth, and diffuse skin thickening giving an orange-peel (peau d'orange) appearance over 3 weeks, without a discrete palpable lump. Skin biopsy shows tumor emboli within dermal lymphatics. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
opts: Wide local excision with sentinel lymph node biopsy
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by modified radical mastectomy
why: Upfront surgery has poor outcomes and is not standard in inflammatory breast cancer
Breast conservation and sentinel node biopsy are contraindicated in inflammatory breast cancer
Hormonal therapy alone is inadequate for this aggressive, locally advanced disease
Correct: neoadjuvant chemotherapy is standard first-line treatment
exp: Inflammatory breast carcinoma (dermal lymphatic tumor emboli, rapid peau d'orange, T4d) is a locally advanced, biologically aggressive cancer treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy first; upfront surgery and breast-conserving approaches with SLNB are both avoided.

q: A bedridden 70-year-old man has a sacral wound with full-thickness skin loss where the wound base is completely covered with yellow slough and black eschar, obscuring the true depth of tissue involvement. Which NPUAP stage best classifies this pressure injury?
why: Stage II is partial-thickness with an exposed, visible dermis, not full-thickness with slough
Correct: when slough/eschar obscures the wound base, depth cannot be assessed and it is classified unstageable
Stage III requires a visible wound base, not one obscured by eschar
Deep tissue injury is intact or discolored skin over damaged tissue, not an open sloughy wound
exp: A pressure injury is classified unstageable, regardless of how deep it may ultimately prove to be, whenever slough or eschar completely obscures the wound base and true depth cannot be assessed; staging resumes only after debridement.

q: A man with poorly controlled diabetes, aged 58, presents with high-grade fever, right upper quadrant pain, and tender hepatomegaly. Imaging reveals multiple small hepatic abscesses; blood culture grows Klebsiella pneumoniae, and stool microscopy/serology are negative for Entamoeba. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Oral metronidazole alone for 10 days, as for amoebic liver abscess
Observation only, as pyogenic abscesses resolve spontaneously with antibiotics
Image-guided percutaneous drainage combined with appropriate systemic antibiotics
why: Metronidazole alone is adequate for typical solitary amoebic abscess, not pyogenic disease
Antibiotics alone are usually insufficient without source control by drainage
Correct: pyogenic liver abscess generally needs drainage plus antibiotics
Resection is reserved for drainage failure or complex multiloculated disease, not first-line
exp: Pyogenic liver abscess, classically Klebsiella pneumoniae in diabetics and often multiple/small, generally requires image-guided percutaneous drainage in addition to systemic antibiotics for source control, unlike solitary amoebic abscesses which often respond to metronidazole alone.

q: A 72-year-old man presents with sudden painless bright red rectal bleeding without prior abdominal pain or fever. He is hemodynamically stable. What is the most likely cause of his lower GI bleeding, and the appropriate next step if bleeding is brisk and colonoscopic view is obscured?
opts: Diverticular bleeding is most likely; CT angiography or a tagged RBC scan can localize the site if colonoscopy fails
Diverticulitis is most likely; broad-spectrum antibiotics are the next step
Ischemic colitis is most likely; observation is sufficient
Colonic malignancy is most likely and requires urgent laparotomy
why: Correct: diverticulosis is the most common cause of painless lower GI bleeding in the elderly, and angiography/tagged scan localizes the source when endoscopy is limited
Diverticulitis presents with pain and fever, not this painless-bleed picture
Ischemic colitis usually causes pain and needs more than observation
Malignancy is a less common cause of acute massive painless bleeding and does not need immediate laparotomy as a first step
exp: Painless, sudden, bright-red lower GI bleeding in an elderly patient is classically diverticular (not diverticulitis, which is painful and inflammatory); when active bleeding obscures the endoscopic view, CT angiography or tagged RBC scintigraphy localizes the source for targeted embolization or surgery.

q: A 40-year-old man complains of recurrent painful swelling beneath the jaw that worsens dramatically during meals and subsides gradually afterward. Examination reveals a firm, tender submandibular gland with a palpable stone at the floor of the mouth. What is the most likely diagnosis and definitive investigation?
opts: Ranula; excision of the sublingual gland
Ludwig's angina; airway securing and IV antibiotics
Sialolithiasis of Wharton's duct; occlusal radiograph or sialography to confirm and localize the stone
why: Parotid swelling is preauricular and does not classically follow this meal-related pattern
Ranula is a painless floor-of-mouth cystic swelling, not a meal-triggered painful one
Ludwig's angina is a rapidly spreading floor-of-mouth cellulitis with airway threat, not a chronic recurrent meal-related swelling
Correct: classic meal-time pain and swelling from Wharton's duct obstruction by a stone
exp: Meal-time pain and swelling of the submandibular gland with a palpable floor-of-mouth stone is classic for a Wharton's duct calculus (sialolithiasis); an occlusal radiograph, since most submandibular stones are radio-opaque, or sialography confirms and localizes it.

q: A 2-year-old known case of Tetralogy of Fallot becomes acutely more cyanotic and irritable after a bout of crying, with increasing respiratory rate. On examination, the previously audible pulmonary ejection murmur becomes softer. What is the most appropriate immediate management of this hypercyanotic (Tet) spell?
opts: Knee-chest positioning, 100% oxygen, and morphine sulfate; add propranolol if the spell persists
IV furosemide to reduce pulmonary congestion
Prostaglandin E1 infusion to maintain ductal patency
why: Surgery is not the immediate step for an acute spell
Correct stepwise management of a Tet spell
Furosemide has no role here — this is not a fluid-overload problem
PGE1 maintains ductal patency in neonates with ductal-dependent lesions, not the standard treatment for an acute spell in an established TOF toddler
exp: A Tet spell is driven by dynamic infundibular spasm worsening right-to-left shunting, which is why the pulmonary murmur softens as flow across the RVOT drops. Knee-chest positioning raises systemic vascular resistance and venous return; oxygen and morphine are first-line, with propranolol reserved for spells that persist.

q: A 38-year-old woman presents with central obesity, purple abdominal striae, proximal muscle weakness, and hypertension. Morning serum ACTH is undetectably low, and CT abdomen shows a 2.5 cm unilateral adrenal mass with a normal contralateral gland. What is the most appropriate management, and what perioperative precaution is essential?
opts: Bilateral adrenalectomy with lifelong steroid replacement
Medical management with ketoconazole alone; surgery is not indicated
Unilateral laparoscopic adrenalectomy, with perioperative glucocorticoid coverage because the contralateral gland is suppressed
External beam radiotherapy to the adrenal mass
why: Bilateral adrenalectomy is reserved for bilateral disease or failed unilateral surgery
Medical therapy is a bridge, not definitive treatment for a resectable adenoma
Correct: unilateral adrenalectomy with steroid cover for the suppressed contralateral gland
Radiotherapy has no role in a resectable functioning adrenal adenoma
exp: Suppressed ACTH with a unilateral cortisol-secreting adenoma means the contralateral adrenal has been chronically suppressed by negative feedback; after removing the functioning adenoma, perioperative and tapering steroid cover is mandatory to prevent an acute adrenal crisis until that gland recovers.

q: Parents bring their 18-month-old child with fusion of the index and middle fingers of the right hand (simple, incomplete syndactyly) for surgical opinion. The two fingers are otherwise unaffected, with no other anomalies. What is the most appropriate timing for surgical separation?
opts: Elective release around 12-18 months of age, before school age - central digit syndactyly does not need earlier surgery
Immediate surgery in the neonatal period regardless of which digits are involved
Delay surgery until after 10 years of age for a better cosmetic outcome
No surgery is needed, as syndactyly resolves spontaneously
why: Correct - central digit pairs follow the standard 12-18 month timing.
Unwarranted early anesthesia risk; early surgery is reserved for the thumb-index/ring-little exception, not central digits.
Delaying this long risks progressively worse deformity and functional/psychological impact.
Syndactyly does not resolve spontaneously and requires surgical separation.
exp: Simple syndactyly between two central digits (e.g., index-middle or middle-ring) that grow at similar rates is typically released around 12-18 months, before fine motor demands increase. Thumb-index and ring-little finger pairs warrant earlier release (about 3-6 months) because of a growth-rate mismatch that causes progressive angulation as the longer digit outgrows the shorter one - this exception does not apply to a central pair like index-middle.

q: A 24-year-old mechanic sustains a clean-cut injury to the volar aspect of his right index finger between the distal palmar crease and the PIP joint while using a grinder, with inability to flex the DIP joint. Which zone of flexor tendon injury is this, notorious for poor outcomes after primary repair?
why: Zone II - correct, tight fibro-osseous tunnel with both FDS and FDP, classically poor healing from adhesions.
Zone V (wrist/forearm) often has associated nerve/vessel injury but tendon repair itself usually does well.
Zone III (palm) has good vascularity and better outcomes than Zone II.
Zone I is distal to FDS insertion with only FDP present, generally better prognosis.
exp: Zone II ('no man's land') runs from the A1 pulley to the FDS insertion; both FDS and FDP lie together in a tight fibro-osseous sheath here, making primary repair prone to adhesions and re-rupture, hence the need for early controlled mobilisation protocols.

q: On day 3 after laparoscopic cholecystectomy, a 45-year-old woman develops bilious fluid draining from the sub-hepatic drain and right upper quadrant pain. MRCP shows a cystic duct stump leak with the common bile duct intact. Which Strasberg classification grade is this?
why: Type A - correct, cystic stump/minor radicle leak with ductal continuity preserved.
Type E is a major bile duct injury needing hepaticojejunostomy - not this case.
Type B is occlusion of an aberrant right hepatic duct, may be silent or cause segmental atrophy.
Type D is a lateral injury to a major duct with continuity preserved, may need repair/drain.
exp: Strasberg Type A is the commonest post-cholecystectomy bile leak - from the cystic duct stump or a minor hepatic radicle - with the main biliary tree intact; usually managed by ERCP with sphincterotomy and stenting rather than reoperation.

q: Ten days after difficult adhesiolysis for small bowel obstruction, a 52-year-old man develops a discharging abdominal wound with 800 mL/day of enteric content through the drain site, worsening after oral feeds. What is the single most important initial step in managing this high-output enterocutaneous fistula?
opts: Sepsis control (drain collections, correct fluid/electrolyte imbalance), then skin protection and nutritional optimisation, allowing up to 4-6 weeks for possible spontaneous closure before definitive surgery
Total parenteral nutrition alone, without imaging or sepsis control
why: Correct - SNAP protocol leads with sepsis control (drain collections, correct fluid/electrolyte imbalance), then nutrition and anatomical definition, with up to a 4-6 week window for spontaneous closure before definitive surgery.
Antibiotics alone do not close a fistula and are not the primary strategy.
Nutrition matters but must be combined with sepsis control and anatomical definition, not used in isolation.
Early surgery in an inflamed, adherent abdomen has high leak/mortality risk unless uncontrolled sepsis forces it.
exp: Enterocutaneous fistula management follows SNAP - Sepsis control, Nutrition, Anatomy definition, Planned surgery - with a 4-6 week window for spontaneous closure before attempting definitive repair; early re-operation in a hostile abdomen carries high morbidity.

q: A 19-year-old college student presents with 4 days of worsening sore throat, trismus, a muffled 'hot potato' voice, and uvular deviation to the left with a bulge above the left tonsil. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
opts: CT neck mandatory before any intervention
Needle aspiration or incision and drainage of the peritonsillar space plus antibiotics
why: CT is not mandatory for a classic clinical presentation, reserved for diagnostic doubt.
Tonsillectomy 'a chaud' is not first-line; reserved for recurrent or complicated cases.
Correct - drainage plus antibiotics is standard of care for peritonsillar abscess.
Antibiotics alone are insufficient for a drainable abscess.
exp: Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) is a clinical diagnosis (trismus, hot-potato voice, uvular deviation, tonsillar bulge); drainage combined with antibiotics is standard of care, with CT reserved for diagnostic uncertainty or suspected deep-space extension.

q: A 58-year-old man in cardiogenic shock after anterior STEMI is being considered for intra-aortic balloon pump support to improve coronary perfusion. Which of the following is an absolute contraindication to IABP insertion?
why: Correct - diastolic balloon inflation in severe AR drives more regurgitant flow into the LV, worsening failure.
Age alone is not a contraindication.
Prior CABG does not preclude IABP use.
Cardiogenic shock is an indication for IABP, not a contraindication.
exp: The IABP inflates in diastole to augment coronary perfusion and deflates in systole to reduce afterload; in severe AR, diastolic inflation worsens regurgitant flow - an absolute contraindication, along with aortic dissection.

subject: Surgery
q: A 40-year-old woman's thyroid FNAC report reads 'atypia of undetermined significance' with scattered follicular cell atypia insufficient for a follicular neoplasm category. Which Bethesda category is this, and what is the recommended next step?
opts: Bethesda V - suspicious for malignancy, proceed to surgery
Bethesda III (AUS/FLUS) - repeat FNAC or molecular testing
why: Bethesda V warrants surgery directly, not repeat sampling.
Bethesda VI is unequivocally malignant on cytology.
Correct - AUS/FLUS carries ~10-30% malignancy risk, recommend repeat sampling.
Bethesda II is benign, follow-up only - doesn't fit the atypia described.
exp: Bethesda III (Atypia/Follicular lesion of Undetermined Significance) carries roughly a 10-30% malignancy risk; guidelines recommend repeat FNAC or molecular testing rather than immediate definitive surgery.

q: A 55-year-old woman, five years after axillary lymph node dissection and radiotherapy for breast cancer, presents with irreversible non-pitting swelling of the arm that does not reduce with limb elevation or compression garments overnight. Which ISL (International Society of Lymphology) stage best describes this?
opts: Stage III - lymphostatic elephantiasis with skin changes
Stage 0 - latent, subclinical lymphatic impairment with no visible oedema
Stage II - non-pitting oedema with fibrosis, not resolved by elevation alone
Stage I - pitting oedema that resolves with limb elevation
why: Stage III adds gross skin/elephantiasis changes not described here.
Stage 0 is subclinical with no visible swelling - doesn't fit.
Correct - non-pitting, fibrotic, elevation-unresponsive oedema.
Stage I resolves with elevation, contrary to this case.
exp: ISL Stage II lymphoedema features tissue fibrosis and non-pitting oedema no longer reversible with elevation alone (unlike Stage I, which pits and reduces with elevation); Stage III adds elephantiasis and skin changes such as papillomatosis.

q: A 60-year-old diabetic man on hemodialysis develops progressively worsening back pain, fever, and new bilateral lower-limb weakness over 5 days, with MRI spine showing a posterior epidural collection compressing the thecal sac at T10-T11. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
opts: Urgent surgical decompression (laminectomy) combined with prolonged antibiotics
IV antibiotics alone with serial MRI monitoring
why: Correct - new neurological deficit from spinal epidural abscess is a surgical emergency.
Aspiration alone is inadequate when there is cord compression.
Antibiotics-alone is reserved for patients without neurological deficit or poor surgical candidates under close monitoring - not this case.
Grossly inadequate, risks permanent paralysis.
exp: Spinal epidural abscess with a new neurological deficit is a surgical emergency; urgent decompressive laminectomy and drainage plus prolonged antibiotics (typically 6-8 weeks) prevents progression to permanent paralysis - outcome correlates strongly with time from deficit onset to surgery.

q: Endoscopy in a 62-year-old man with dysphagia shows a tumour centred 3 cm proximal to the gastroesophageal junction, with its epicentre within the distal oesophagus. Which Siewert type adenocarcinoma of the oesophagogastric junction is this, and what does it guide?
opts: Siewert IV - fundal cancer, not a recognised Siewert category
Siewert I - true oesophageal adenocarcinoma, treated as oesophageal cancer
why: Type III is centred below the GEJ.
Not a standard Siewert category - classification only has types I-III.
Type II is centred at/near the cardia itself, not 3 cm proximal.
Correct - epicentre 1-5 cm above the GEJ, arises from Barrett's, managed as oesophageal cancer.
exp: Siewert type I tumours (epicentre 1-5 cm above the GEJ) arise from Barrett's oesophagus and are managed as oesophageal cancer with oesophagectomy; type II and III are managed more like gastric cancer with extended or total gastrectomy.

q: A 58-year-old multiparous woman reports involuntary leakage of urine on coughing and sneezing but no leakage with sudden urge or between voids. Urodynamic studies would most likely show leakage at what point, confirming stress urinary incontinence?
opts: Involuntary detrusor contraction during bladder filling
Leakage occurring with raised intra-abdominal pressure, without any detrusor contraction
Leakage only during bladder filling at rest with no provocation
why: Suggests overflow incontinence/retention, not stress incontinence.
Describes urge incontinence (detrusor overactivity), not stress incontinence.
Correct - leakage with raised intra-abdominal pressure and no detrusor contraction.
Not a recognised incontinence pattern.
exp: Stress urinary incontinence results from urethral sphincter/pelvic floor weakness; urodynamics show leakage with raised intra-abdominal pressure (cough, sneeze, exertion) without a detrusor contraction, distinguishing it from urge incontinence.

q: A neonate born to a mother who took lithium during pregnancy develops cyanosis and a wide, fixed split S2 with a holosystolic murmur. Echocardiography shows apical displacement of the tricuspid valve leaflets with atrialisation of the right ventricle. What is the diagnosis?
why: ToF has a boot-shaped heart with pulmonary stenosis, VSD, overriding aorta - different echo picture.
Correct - apical tricuspid leaflet displacement with RV atrialisation, linked to maternal lithium exposure.
Truncus arteriosus shows a single arterial trunk overriding a VSD.
TGA presents with severe cyanosis and parallel great vessels on echo, not tricuspid displacement.
exp: Ebstein's anomaly is defined by apical displacement of the septal and posterior tricuspid leaflets, 'atrialising' part of the right ventricle; classically associated with maternal lithium exposure and can present with cyanosis, heart failure, and WPW-related arrhythmias.

q: A 68-year-old man presents with exertional syncope and a harsh ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids, with a soft/absent second heart sound. Echocardiography shows a calcified aortic valve with an area of 0.8 cm² and an ejection fraction of 45%. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Balloon aortic valvuloplasty as definitive therapy
Continue medical management and reassess in 6 months
why: valvuloplasty is a bridge measure, restenosis is near-universal in adults, not definitive
watchful waiting is inappropriate once symptomatic with reduced EF — mortality is high without intervention
beta-blockers reduce contractility and can precipitate decompensation against a fixed outflow obstruction
correct.
exp: Severe aortic stenosis (valve area <1.0 cm²) with symptoms (syncope) or reduced EF (<50%) is a class I indication for aortic valve replacement (surgical or TAVR depending on surgical risk); balloon valvuloplasty is only temporizing/palliative, and medical therapy does not alter the fatal natural history once symptoms appear.

q: A 55-year-old woman with long-standing Hashimoto's thyroiditis on levothyroxine presents with a rapidly enlarging, firm thyroid mass over 3 weeks with new dysphagia and dyspnoea. FNAC is inconclusive. Which underlying malignancy must be specifically excluded given her history?
why: correct
MTC arises from parafollicular C cells, unrelated to autoimmune thyroiditis, linked to MEN2/RET
papillary carcinoma is the commonest thyroid cancer but grows slowly and is not specifically linked to this rapid-growth pattern
follicular carcinoma spreads haematogenously and links to iodine deficiency, not Hashimoto's.
exp: Hashimoto's thyroiditis is a strong risk factor for primary thyroid lymphoma (usually diffuse large B-cell type); rapid growth of a long-standing goitre with compressive symptoms in a Hashimoto's patient should prompt core biopsy/flow cytometry, since FNAC alone often cannot distinguish lymphoma from thyroiditis or anaplastic carcinoma.

subject: Surgery
q: A carpenter presents 2 days after a puncture wound to the palm with the finger held in slight flexion, uniform fusiform swelling, tenderness along the entire flexor tendon sheath, and severe pain on passive extension of the finger. Which condition is this, and what is the most appropriate immediate management?
opts: Felon — needle aspiration in the clinic
Pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis — urgent surgical drainage plus IV antibiotics
Paronychia — warm soaks and oral antibiotics
why: felon is a pulp-space infection with localized throbbing pain, not sheath-wide swelling, and needs incision not just aspiration
correct
paronychia is a much more localized nail-fold infection, less urgent
Dupuytren's is a chronic fibrosing contracture, not an acute infective emergency.
exp: Kanavel's four cardinal signs (fusiform swelling, flexed posture, tenderness along the sheath, pain on passive extension) diagnose pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis, a surgical emergency; delay risks tendon necrosis and irreversible hand dysfunction, so urgent sheath irrigation/drainage plus IV antibiotics is mandatory.

subject: Surgery
q: A 45-year-old man presents with acute-onset bilateral leg weakness, saddle-area numbness, and urinary retention with overflow incontinence after lifting a heavy weight. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate step?
opts: Elective MRI as an outpatient within 2 weeks
Urgent MRI whole spine and surgical decompression within 48 hours
Bed rest with a lumbar corset for 6 weeks
why: conservative management risks permanent neurological/sphincteric damage in a true surgical emergency
outpatient elective imaging is far too delayed for a time-critical diagnosis
correct
bed rest does not address the compressive lesion and allows further deterioration.
exp: Cauda equina syndrome (bilateral leg weakness/pain, saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction) is a surgical emergency, typically from a large central disc prolapse; delay beyond about 48 hours from onset of bladder/bowel involvement is associated with significantly worse recovery of continence and motor function, so urgent MRI and decompression are mandated.

subject: Surgery
q: A 68-year-old woman presents with severe epigastric/chest pain, retching without production of vomitus, and a nasogastric tube cannot be passed beyond the lower oesophagus. Chest X-ray shows a retrocardiac air-fluid level. What is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate next step?
opts: Achalasia cardia — start calcium channel blockers
Boerhaave syndrome — chest tube drainage alone
Gastric volvulus (paraesophageal hernia) — urgent surgical reduction and repair
why: achalasia presents with progressive dysphagia, not acute retching with an impassable NG tube
Boerhaave syndrome is oesophageal perforation from forceful vomiting, presenting with subcutaneous emphysema/Hamman's crunch, and needs repair not chest tube alone
sigmoid volvulus is a large-bowel problem presenting with abdominal distension, not epigastric/retrocardiac findings
correct.
exp: Borchardt's triad (severe epigastric pain, retching without vomitus, inability to pass a nasogastric tube) is classic for gastric volvulus, usually from a large paraesophageal hiatus hernia; it is a surgical emergency because of strangulation/necrosis risk, requiring urgent reduction and hernia repair (often with gastropexy).

subject: Surgery
q: A 55-year-old man has an incidentally detected renal cyst on ultrasound. CT shows a cyst with a few thin septations and minimal enhancement, classified as Bosniak category II-F. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Reassure and discharge with no follow-up
why: correct
surgery is overtreatment for a II-F lesion
aspiration/sclerotherapy is not recommended for a potentially neoplastic complex cyst
discharging without follow-up risks missing malignant progression, since II-F carries a non-trivial risk.
exp: The Bosniak classification stratifies renal cystic lesions by malignancy risk on contrast CT; category II-F ("follow") lesions have minimally complex features (a few thin septa, minimal enhancement) with a small but real malignancy risk, needing periodic surveillance imaging, while surgery is reserved for categories III (surgical grey zone) and IV (clearly malignant-appearing).

subject: Surgery
q: Five days after hip surgery, a 55-year-old patient develops sudden dyspnoea, tachycardia, and hypotension. CT pulmonary angiography confirms a large bilateral pulmonary embolism, and echocardiography shows right ventricular dilatation with septal flattening. Blood pressure is 80/50 mmHg despite fluids. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
opts: Therapeutic-dose low molecular weight heparin alone
why: systemic thrombolysis is normally first-line for massive PE, but recent major surgery (post-op day 5) is a relative contraindication due to surgical-site bleeding risk
correct — embolectomy achieves reperfusion without the bleeding risk of systemic lytics in a recent post-operative patient
anticoagulation alone does not lyse existing clot fast enough to reverse shock from a massive embolus
an IVC filter prevents further emboli but does not treat the current life-threatening clot burden.
exp: This is massive PE (hypotension/shock with RV strain), which is normally treated with systemic thrombolysis — but recent major surgery (hip surgery 5 days earlier here) is a recognised contraindication to systemic thrombolysis because of catastrophic surgical-site bleeding risk. In this setting, catheter-directed or surgical pulmonary embolectomy is the preferred reperfusion strategy, treating the same life-threatening clot burden without the systemic lytic bleeding risk.

q: A 32-year-old woman with a confirmed BRCA1 mutation and a strong family history of breast and ovarian cancer asks about risk-reduction options. Which statement about her management is correct?
opts: Screening mammography alone is sufficient; surgery offers no benefit
Tamoxifen prophylaxis alone eliminates the need for any imaging surveillance
Risk-reducing bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is recommended around age 35–40 (or after childbearing), reducing both ovarian and breast cancer risk
Prophylactic surgery is only indicated after a cancer diagnosis is made
why: high-risk carriers need enhanced surveillance (MRI + mammography) or risk-reducing surgery, not screening alone
tamoxifen may reduce risk but does not replace surveillance imaging
correct
risk-reducing surgery is precisely a pre-emptive option, not restricted to after a cancer diagnosis.
exp: BRCA1/2 carriers have markedly elevated lifetime risk of breast and ovarian cancer; risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy (typically age 35–40 or after childbearing) reduces ovarian cancer risk by roughly 80–90% and also lowers breast cancer risk (via reduced oestrogen exposure), while risk-reducing mastectomy independently cuts breast cancer risk by a similar margin — offered pre-emptively, not after a cancer diagnosis.

q: A patient rescued from a closed-room house fire has singed nasal hair, soot around the mouth and nose, carbonaceous sputum, and a hoarse voice, though he is currently maintaining oxygen saturation on room air. What is the most appropriate immediate step?
opts: High-flow oxygen alone and hourly monitoring
Early elective intubation before airway oedema progresses
why: waiting for desaturation risks a sudden, unmanageable airway loss as oedema peaks
oxygen alone does not address impending mechanical airway obstruction
escharotomy treats circumferential chest/neck eschar restricting ventilation, a different mechanism/indication than airway oedema
correct.
exp: Signs of inhalational injury (singed vibrissae, carbonaceous sputum, hoarseness, perioral soot) predict progressive airway oedema over the following hours even when current saturation is normal; early elective intubation while the airway is still patent is safer than waiting for decompensation, when intubation may become difficult or impossible.

q: A 45-year-old woman in the ICU after major trauma develops fever and right upper quadrant tenderness with a positive Murphy's sign. Ultrasound shows no gallstones, a gallbladder wall of only 2 mm, and no pericholecystic fluid — findings that do not meet imaging criteria for cholecystitis despite the clinical picture. What is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis?
opts: Hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid (HIDA) scan showing non-visualization of the gallbladder
MRCP to look for common bile duct stones
Diagnostic laparoscopy as the first-line test
why: correct — HIDA is the standard next test when ultrasound is equivocal but clinical suspicion for cholecystitis (here, acalculous, in a critically ill patient) remains high
repeating ultrasound delays diagnosis and treatment in a critically ill patient
MRCP evaluates the bile ducts for stones/strictures, not gallbladder function/cystic duct obstruction
diagnostic laparoscopy is invasive and not the first-line confirmatory test when a non-invasive nuclear scan is available.
exp: Acute acalculous cholecystitis in critically ill patients often has a non-diagnostic ultrasound (no stones, normal or near-normal wall thickness) despite a strong clinical picture; here ultrasound does not meet Tokyo Guidelines imaging criteria, so a HIDA scan is the appropriate next step — non-visualization of the gallbladder within about 60 minutes (from cystic duct obstruction/oedema) confirms the diagnosis with high sensitivity/specificity.

q: A 5-day-old neonate presents with sudden onset of bilious vomiting and abdominal distension. He was passing normal stools until today. Upper GI contrast study shows a corkscrew appearance of the duodenum. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Conservative management with nasogastric decompression and observation
Emergency laparotomy (Ladd's procedure) for malrotation with midgut volvulus
Barium enema as both diagnostic and therapeutic
Elective surgery after confirming with a CT abdomen
why: conservative management risks bowel infarction in a time-critical emergency
correct
barium enema is used for suspected Hirschsprung's disease or intussusception, not malrotation
awaiting elective CT delays a true emergency when the diagnosis is already confirmed.
exp: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is a surgical emergency until proven otherwise; the corkscrew sign on upper GI contrast confirms malrotation with midgut volvulus, which can infarct the entire midgut within hours if untreated — emergency laparotomy (Ladd's procedure: counter-clockwise detorsion, division of Ladd's bands, appendectomy) is mandatory.

q: A child with a supracondylar humerus fracture in an above-elbow cast complains of severe, worsening forearm pain unrelieved by analgesia; radial pulse is still palpable. Which finding should prompt immediate cast removal rather than waiting for pulselessness?
opts: Pain out of proportion to injury, worsened by passive finger extension
why: Correct - pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch are the earliest, most sensitive signs.
Pulselessness is a very late sign; the pulse is often preserved despite established compartment syndrome.
Pallor appears later as ischaemia progresses.
Paralysis reflects advanced nerve/muscle ischaemia, also late.
exp: In compartment syndrome, pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch are the earliest signs; pulse, pallor, and paralysis are late findings, and waiting for pulselessness risks Volkmann's ischaemic contracture.

q: A 6-week-old has persistent conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, pale stools, and dark urine. HIDA shows no bowel excretion; intraoperative cholangiogram confirms biliary atresia. What single factor most determines surgical success?
opts: Performing Kasai portoenterostomy before 8-10 weeks of age
Deliberately delaying surgery until 6 months for anaesthesia fitness
why: Birth weight is not the key prognostic driver.
Correct - native liver survival falls sharply the later surgery is performed.
Ursodeoxycholic acid is an adjunct for bile flow, not a substitute for timely surgery.
Deliberate delay worsens outcome.
exp: Native liver survival after Kasai portoenterostomy depends heavily on age at surgery, falling sharply beyond roughly 8-10 weeks - early referral and surgery are the single most important prognostic factors.

q: A 50-year-old with epigastric pain undergoes endoscopic biopsy of a gastric ulcer showing low-grade gastric MALT lymphoma; rapid urease test is positive and disease is confined to the stomach wall. Best initial treatment?
why: Gastrectomy is not first-line for this indolent, H. pylori-driven lymphoma.
Chemotherapy is reserved for eradication failure or advanced disease.
Correct - eradication alone achieves regression in most early localized cases.
Radiotherapy is second-line after eradication failure.
exp: Localized low-grade gastric MALT lymphoma is strongly H. pylori-associated, and first-line treatment is eradication therapy alone, reserving chemo/radiotherapy/surgery for non-responders or advanced disease.

subject: Surgery
q: A 14-year-old boy has recurrent profuse epistaxis and progressive nasal obstruction. CT shows a vascular nasopharyngeal mass widening the pterygopalatine fossa with anterior bowing of the posterior maxillary sinus wall. Diagnosis and correct next step?
opts: Antral choanal polyp; simple avulsion in OPD
Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma; avoid biopsy, image and consider embolization before excision
why: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma occurs in older adults; biopsy there is safe, unlike JNA.
A choanal polyp does not show this vascular/bony CT pattern.
Rhinosporidiosis is a friable polypoidal mass without this CT pattern.
Correct - antral bowing and pterygopalatine widening (Holman-Miller sign) are classic JNA; biopsy risks catastrophic bleeding.
exp: JNA is a highly vascular benign tumour of adolescent males; diagnosis is radiological (Holman-Miller sign), biopsy is avoided, and preoperative embolization reduces intraoperative blood loss before excision.

subject: Surgery
q: A 24-year-old woman has malaise, low-grade fever, absent left radial and brachial pulses, and a 30 mmHg blood pressure difference between arms, with markedly elevated ESR. Most likely diagnosis?
why: Correct - large-vessel vasculitis in a young woman with absent pulses and elevated ESR is classic Takayasu.
Coarctation is congenital, present from birth/childhood, not an ESR-raising illness.
Buerger's affects young male smokers with distal small/medium vessels, not the aortic arch.
Giant cell arteritis affects older adults, typically temporal arteries.
exp: Takayasu arteritis is a large-vessel vasculitis predominantly in young Asian/Indian women, causing aortic arch branch stenosis with absent pulses and inter-limb BP discrepancy, with raised inflammatory markers in the active phase.

subject: Surgery
q: Six hours after total thyroidectomy, a patient develops rapidly increasing neck swelling, stridor, and respiratory distress at the bedside. What is the immediate life-saving step before transfer to theatre?
opts: Await portable CT neck to confirm haematoma
Open the wound immediately at the bedside to evacuate the haematoma
Perform emergency tracheostomy as the first step
why: Imaging delays a true airway emergency and should never be first.
Correct - bedside wound opening decompresses the haematoma and can be life-saving before intubation or theatre.
Steroids do not relieve mechanical compression fast enough.
Tracheostomy through a haematoma-distorted neck is difficult and not the first step.
exp: A rapidly expanding post-thyroidectomy neck haematoma causes airway obstruction from tracheal compression and mucosal venous congestion; opening the wound at the bedside is the immediate decompressive step.

subject: Surgery
q: A patient has a 2 cm full-thickness defect over the nasal tip after basal cell carcinoma excision, with exposed cartilage; nasolabial and bilobed flaps are judged insufficient for coverage and colour match. Which flap, based on the supratrochlear artery, is the workhorse reconstruction?
why: Rhomboid flaps suit small cheek/lateral facial defects.
Nasolabial flaps suit alar/lateral defects but lack arc/bulk for tip loss with cartilage exposure.
Correct - based on the axial supratrochlear artery, it is the gold-standard for large/full-thickness nasal tip defects.
Bilobed flaps suit smaller dorsum/sidewall defects.
exp: The paramedian forehead flap, based on the supratrochlear artery, provides robust colour-matched tissue for large nasal tip/dorsum defects and is the workhorse reconstruction, typically staged with pedicle division at 3 weeks.

subject: Surgery
q: A 68-year-old man has a progressive wide-based shuffling gait, urinary incontinence, and mild cognitive decline over 6 months. MRI shows ventriculomegaly disproportionate to sulcal atrophy; LP opening pressure is normal, and gait improves after a large-volume CSF tap. Diagnosis?
why: Alzheimer's presents with early prominent memory loss and cortical atrophy, not a positive tap-test response.
Chronic subdural shows a crescentic extra-axial collection, not symmetric ventriculomegaly.
Parkinson's shows tremor/rigidity/bradykinesia and does not respond to CSF removal.
Correct - the gait, incontinence, dementia triad with normal pressure and a positive tap test is classic NPH.
exp: Normal pressure hydrocephalus presents with the triad of gait apraxia, urinary incontinence, and dementia with normal CSF opening pressure; a positive large-volume tap test predicts benefit from VP shunting.

subject: Surgery
q: A 55-year-old has a submucosal gastric mass found on endoscopy; biopsy shows spindle cells, immunohistochemistry positive for CD117 (c-KIT). Diagnosis and key treatment implication?
opts: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST) - surgical resection, imatinib for high-risk/metastatic disease
Gastric MALT lymphoma - H. pylori eradication
why: Correct - CD117 positivity with spindle cells is the hallmark of GIST from the interstitial cells of Cajal.
Adenocarcinoma is epithelial, not spindle-cell/CD117-positive.
MALT lymphoma is CD20-positive lymphoid tissue, not spindle cells.
Carcinoid shows chromogranin/synaptophysin, not CD117.
exp: CD117 (c-KIT) positivity on immunohistochemistry defines GIST; complete resection is mainstay for localized disease, with imatinib used for high-risk, unresectable, or metastatic tumours.

subject: Surgery
q: A 45-year-old with gout has recurrent flank pain; plain KUB X-ray shows no calculus, but ultrasound reveals a right renal stone. Urine pH is persistently 5.0. Best medical measure to treat and prevent recurrence?
why: Calcium intake is unrelated to uric acid stone chemistry.
Correct - alkalinizing urine to pH 6.5-7 dissolves uric acid stones and prevents recurrence.
Thiazides reduce urinary calcium in calcium-oxalate stone formers, not uric acid stones.
PCNL is reserved for large/refractory stones, not first-line when medical dissolution is possible.
exp: Uric acid stones are radiolucent (seen on ultrasound/CT, not X-ray) and form in acidic urine; alkalinizing with potassium citrate to pH 6.5-7 both dissolves existing stones and prevents recurrence.

subject: Surgery
q: A 40-year-old with prior tuberculosis has progressive ascites, pedal oedema, and raised JVP that paradoxically rises further on inspiration. Echo shows pericardial thickening with normal ventricular systolic function. Diagnosis?
why: Tamponade shows pulsus paradoxus and effusion, not Kussmaul's sign or pericardial thickening.
Restrictive cardiomyopathy is a myocardial, not pericardial, pathology.
Correct - a rigid TB-thickened pericardium prevents accommodating inspiratory venous return, producing Kussmaul's sign.
RV infarction does not produce this inspiratory JVP pattern.
exp: Kussmaul's sign - a paradoxical rise in JVP on inspiration - occurs in constrictive pericarditis; TB is a leading cause in India, and definitive treatment is pericardiectomy.

subject: Surgery
q: A diabetic man with poor glycaemic control develops rapidly spreading erythema and oedema over his leg over 18 hours, accompanied by pain strikingly out of proportion to the visible skin findings, palpable crepitus, and haemorrhagic bullae, along with fever and tachycardia. What is the most likely diagnosis, and the single most important immediate management step?
opts: Cellulitis; start IV antibiotics and observe for 24-48 hours before further action
Deep vein thrombosis with venous stasis changes; anticoagulation
Necrotising fasciitis; emergency aggressive surgical debridement without delay
Compartment syndrome; elevation and serial neurovascular checks only
why: Cellulitis does not cause crepitus, disproportionate pain, or haemorrhagic bullae; a wait-and-watch approach would be dangerous if necrotising fasciitis is actually present
DVT causes unilateral limb swelling and pain but not crepitus, bullae, systemic sepsis, or rapidly progressive skin necrosis
Correct — this picture demands emergency surgical debridement, the single most outcome-determining step
Compartment syndrome causes pain out of proportion and tense swelling but not crepitus, bullae, or infective/toxic features; it requires fasciotomy, not observation
exp: Pain disproportionate to exam findings, rapidly progressive erythema, crepitus, and haemorrhagic bullae in a diabetic patient are red-flag features for necrotising fasciitis, a surgical emergency; early, aggressive surgical debridement of all necrotic tissue is the single intervention proven to reduce mortality — delaying surgery for imaging or antibiotic trials worsens outcomes.

q: A 48-year-old obese woman has recurrent episodes of dull right-upper-quadrant/epigastric pain after fatty meals, each lasting under 4-6 hours and resolving completely between episodes. She is afebrile, has a normal white cell count and normal liver function tests, and ultrasound shows gallstones with a gallbladder wall thickness of 2 mm and no pericholecystic fluid. What is the most likely diagnosis, and how does it differ from acute cholecystitis?
opts: Biliary colic; pain resolves within hours without gallbladder wall inflammation (no thickening, fever, or leukocytosis), unlike acute cholecystitis where sustained cystic duct obstruction causes true inflammation
Acute cholecystitis; requires immediate laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 24 hours regardless of imaging findings
Choledocholithiasis; requires urgent ERCP for common bile duct clearance
Chronic pancreatitis; requires a modified Puestow procedure
why: Correct — textbook biliary colic, distinguished from cholecystitis by the absence of inflammatory findings and rapid resolution
The absence of fever, leukocytosis, and wall thickening/pericholecystic fluid argues against acute cholecystitis, which needs those inflammatory findings before urgent cholecystectomy is indicated
Choledocholithiasis typically causes deranged LFTs from bile duct obstruction, absent here
Chronic pancreatitis causes chronic epigastric pain often with steatorrhoea/weight loss and pancreatic ductal changes on imaging, not this gallstone-related biliary colic picture
exp: Biliary colic results from transient cystic duct obstruction by a stone that then dislodges, causing self-limited pain without ongoing inflammation — hence normal inflammatory markers and a thin, normal gallbladder wall on ultrasound; acute cholecystitis results from persistent obstruction causing true gallbladder wall inflammation, with fever, leukocytosis, and sonographic wall thickening or pericholecystic fluid.

q: A 68-year-old man develops crampy left-sided abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea three days after emergency repair of a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm; colonoscopy shows mucosal congestion and ulceration confined to the splenic flexure. Which vascular basis best explains this finding?
opts: Watershed ischemia at the junction of SMA and IMA territories (Griffith's point)
Embolic occlusion of the superior mesenteric artery
Occlusion of the inferior rectal artery
why: Correct — splenic flexure (Griffith's point) is the SMA-IMA watershed, most vulnerable after IMA sacrifice/hypoperfusion during aortic surgery.
SMA embolism causes acute mesenteric ischemia with pain out of proportion to exam, affecting small bowel/right colon, not an isolated splenic-flexure pattern.
Portal vein thrombosis causes bowel congestion typically with ascites/varices, not localized splenic-flexure colitis post-AAA repair.
The inferior rectal artery supplies the anal canal below the pectinate line, unrelated to colonic watershed ischemia.
exp: The splenic flexure is a watershed zone supplied by the terminal branches of both the SMA (middle colic) and IMA (left colic), making it most vulnerable to hypoperfusion after aortic surgery when IMA flow is sacrificed or collateral flow is marginal — ischemic colitis here is a recognised complication of AAA repair and should prompt urgent flexible sigmoidoscopy.

q: A 6-month-old infant presents with a soft, non-tender, brilliantly transilluminant swelling in the posterior triangle of the neck that has been slowly enlarging since birth, with no signs of inflammation. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Branchial cyst classically presents in the anterior triangle at the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid in a young adult, not the posterior triangle of an infant.
Thyroglossal duct cyst is midline and moves with tongue protrusion/swallowing, not lateral in the posterior triangle.
Correct — posterior triangle location plus brilliant transillumination in infancy is characteristic of cystic hygroma.
Sternocleidomastoid tumour of infancy is a firm, non-transilluminant mass within the muscle belly itself, associated with torticollis.
exp: Cystic hygroma is a congenital lymphatic malformation classically found in the posterior triangle, brilliantly transilluminant because it is filled with lymph rather than solid tissue or pus — it can be associated with Turner syndrome/nuchal translucency on antenatal scan and needs MRI plus sclerotherapy or excision.

q: A young woman presents with sudden painful swelling of the left leg with no preceding trauma; Doppler confirms left iliofemoral deep vein thrombosis, and CT venography shows compression of the left common iliac vein by the overlying right common iliac artery against the vertebral body. What is this anatomical predisposition called?
why: Leriche syndrome is aortoiliac occlusive disease causing claudication, impotence and absent femoral pulses, not an anatomical vein-compression syndrome.
Nutcracker syndrome is compression of the left renal vein between the aorta and SMA, causing haematuria/flank pain, not leg DVT.
Paget-Schroetter syndrome is effort thrombosis of the subclavian/axillary vein in the upper limb, not the iliac vein.
Correct — right common iliac artery compresses the left common iliac vein, predisposing to left iliofemoral DVT.
exp: May-Thurner syndrome is compression of the left common iliac vein between the right common iliac artery and the lumbar vertebra, predisposing young women particularly to left-sided iliofemoral DVT — recognising it matters because these patients need venous stenting in addition to anticoagulation to prevent post-thrombotic syndrome.

q: A patient with biochemically confirmed primary hyperparathyroidism undergoes neck exploration, but only three parathyroid glands are identified and serum calcium remains elevated postoperatively. Where is a missed superior or inferior gland most likely to be found on re-exploration?
opts: In the anterior mediastinum within thymic tissue
Behind the oesophagus in the retropharyngeal space
why: Correct — shared third-pouch embryology with the thymus makes the anterior mediastinum the commonest site for an ectopic/missed inferior parathyroid.
Intrathyroidal parathyroid glands occur but are a distinctly less common site than the thymus for a missed gland.
The retropharyngeal space is an uncommon site, more typical of a superior gland that has migrated posteriorly, not the leading overall cause of missed glands.
The carotid sheath is not a typical resting site for ectopic parathyroid tissue.
exp: Because the inferior parathyroids share embryological origin (third pharyngeal pouch) with the thymus, a missed inferior gland most often descends into the anterior mediastinum within thymic tissue — this is the single most common site for a missing gland at re-exploration, and preoperative sestamibi/4D-CT localisation is used to find it before reoperating.

q: The parents of a 5-year-old boy with unilateral grade III microtia ask when surgical ear reconstruction with autologous costal cartilage should ideally begin. What is the most appropriate timing consideration?
opts: Immediately in the neonatal period before cartilage ossifies
Only after 18 years of age when facial growth is complete
Around 6 years of age, once the costal cartilage is adequate and the normal ear has reached near-adult size
Timing is irrelevant as long as a prosthetic ear is used instead
why: Neonatal surgery is avoided — there isn't enough costal cartilage bulk yet, and framework survival is poor.
Waiting until 18 is unnecessary and psychosocially disadvantageous; reconstruction is deliberately done in early childhood before schooling-related teasing peaks.
Correct — by ~6 years the normal ear is near-adult sized and costal cartilage is sufficient for framework carving.
A prosthetic ear is an alternative for patients unsuitable for autologous reconstruction, not a reason to ignore optimal surgical timing.
exp: Autologous rib cartilage reconstruction is timed to around 6 years of age because by then the contralateral normal ear has reached roughly 85% of its adult size (allowing a good size match) and the child's costal cartilage framework is large enough to carve a durable ear framework — earlier surgery risks an undersized reconstruction and inadequate donor cartilage.

q: A young man involved in a high-speed road traffic accident remains deeply comatose with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 6 despite an initial CT brain showing no significant mass lesion or midline shift, only a few tiny petechial haemorrhages at the grey-white matter junction. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Extradural haematoma produces a lens-shaped hyperdensity with a lucid interval and mass effect, clearly visible on CT — not this picture.
Acute subdural haematoma shows a crescentic hyperdensity with mass effect on CT, which is absent here.
Simple concussion causes only transient loss of consciousness with rapid recovery, not sustained GCS 6 coma.
Correct — coma out of proportion to a near-normal CT, with grey-white junction petechiae, is the classic description of diffuse axonal injury.
exp: Diffuse axonal injury results from rotational/shearing acceleration-deceleration forces that damage axons diffusely, classically producing coma disproportionate to a deceptively unremarkable CT — MRI (especially gradient-echo/SWI sequences) is far more sensitive, showing petechial haemorrhages at the grey-white junction, corpus callosum and dorsolateral midbrain.

subject: Surgery
q: Three weeks after a Billroth II partial gastrectomy with gastrojejunostomy, a patient develops recurrent postprandial epigastric pain and bloating that is dramatically relieved by an episode of projectile bilious (non-food-containing) vomiting. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Correct — postprandial pain relieved abruptly by projectile bile-only vomiting is the classic description of afferent loop syndrome.
Dumping syndrome causes early postprandial diaphoresis, palpitations and diarrhoea from rapid osmotic fluid shifts, not relief by bilious vomiting.
Alkaline reflux gastritis causes constant burning epigastric pain with bilious vomiting that does NOT relieve the pain, unlike afferent loop syndrome.
Anastomotic stricture causes progressive dysphagia/vomiting of food, not a pattern of pain dramatically relieved by bile-only vomiting.
exp: Afferent loop syndrome occurs when the duodenal (afferent) limb of a Billroth II reconstruction becomes partially obstructed, causing bile and pancreatic secretions to accumulate and distend the loop after meals; the pressure is relieved by sudden, forceful, food-free bilious vomiting that dramatically eases the pain — chronic cases risk blind-loop bacterial overgrowth and B12 deficiency.

q: An asymptomatic 30-year-old undergoes an abdominal ultrasound for an unrelated complaint, which incidentally reveals two renal masses joined across the midline at their lower poles by an isthmus lying anterior to the aorta at the level of L3-L4. This anatomical variant most predisposes to which complication?
opts: Ureteropelvic junction obstruction and stone formation
why: Horseshoe kidney is not specifically linked to renal artery stenosis; its vascular supply is variable and multiple, but stenosis is not the classic complication.
Correct — malrotation with high ureteric insertion predisposes to UPJ obstruction, stasis, infection and calculi.
Renal vein thrombosis is not a recognised complication of horseshoe kidney anatomy.
Horseshoe kidney is a fusion anomaly, unrelated to the genetic cystic disease PKD.
exp: A horseshoe kidney's isthmus is trapped below the inferior mesenteric artery during ascent, leaving the kidneys malrotated with anteriorly placed, high-inserting ureters — this predisposes to UPJ obstruction, stasis and stone formation, and horseshoe kidney also carries an increased risk of Wilms tumour in children.

subject: Surgery
q: A young motorcyclist involved in a high-speed collision arrives with a chest X-ray showing a widened mediastinum and loss of the aortic knob contour, though he is haemodynamically stable. Which site of injury and next step are most appropriate?
opts: Injury at the aortic root; proceed directly to open sternotomy
Injury at the diaphragmatic hiatus; obtain an upper GI contrast study
Injury at the ligamentum arteriosum near the aortic isthmus; obtain CT angiography to confirm before repair
Injury at the innominate artery origin; observe and repeat chest X-ray in 24 hours
why: The aortic root is a rare site for blunt deceleration injury; the isthmus at the ligamentum arteriosum is far more typical.
A widened mediastinum with this mechanism points to aortic injury, not diaphragmatic rupture, which has a different radiographic picture (bowel gas in the chest).
Correct — isthmic injury at the ligamentum arteriosum is classic, and CT angiography confirms the diagnosis in a stable patient before definitive repair.
A stable patient with this finding still needs urgent definitive imaging, not simple observation — untreated transection can rupture catastrophically.
exp: Traumatic aortic injury from sudden deceleration classically shears the aorta at the relatively fixed ligamentum arteriosum near the isthmus (just distal to the left subclavian origin); a widened mediastinum on CXR is a screening clue, but CT angiography is the confirmatory investigation of choice in a stable patient before proceeding to endovascular (TEVAR) or open repair.

subject: Surgery
q: A 58-year-old woman presents with a six-month history of an eczematous, crusted, unilateral nipple-areolar lesion that has not responded to topical steroids, with no discrete palpable breast lump. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Reassure and continue topical steroids for a longer trial
Start empirical antifungal cream for suspected candidal intertrigo
Order only a mammogram and defer biopsy if normal
Perform a full-thickness wedge biopsy of the nipple-areolar complex
why: Failure to respond to steroids over months is itself a red flag that should prompt biopsy, not more of the same treatment.
Paget's disease is frequently misdiagnosed as eczema or fungal dermatitis, which delays diagnosis — persistent unilateral lesions need biopsy, not empirical antifungals.
Mammography can be falsely normal in Paget's disease, especially with an underlying malignancy too small or diffuse to detect, so a normal mammogram does not obviate biopsy.
Correct — biopsy of the nipple-areolar complex is mandatory to look for Paget cells and rule out underlying malignancy.
exp: A unilateral, treatment-resistant eczematous nipple lesion in an older woman must be treated as Paget's disease of the breast until proven otherwise — it is associated with an underlying DCIS or invasive carcinoma in most cases, and a full-thickness nipple biopsy (showing pathognomonic Paget cells) is required for diagnosis regardless of mammographic findings. The exact proportion with underlying malignancy is cited variably (85-95%) across sources.

subject: Surgery
q: A 32-year-old woman presents with rapidly progressive hirsutism, deepening of voice, and cushingoid facies over 4 months. CT abdomen shows a heterogeneous right adrenal mass measuring 9 cm with irregular margins. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Percutaneous CT-guided biopsy of the mass
Observation with repeat imaging in 6 months
why: Correct - open en bloc resection is standard given seeding risk with less invasive approaches
Biopsy risks needle-tract seeding and rarely changes management here
Laparoscopic adrenalectomy is reserved for masses under 6 cm without malignant features
Observation is inappropriate given rapid progression and malignant imaging features
exp: Rapid virilization plus a large (over 6 cm), irregular adrenal mass strongly suggests adrenocortical carcinoma; such masses should be resected via open en bloc adrenalectomy (avoiding capsule rupture) rather than laparoscopically, and percutaneous biopsy is avoided given needle-tract seeding risk.

subject: Surgery
q: A factory worker presents 2 hours after his hand was struck by a grease-gun nozzle. The entry wound on the index finger pulp is small and the finger looks only mildly swollen with minimal pain. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Reassurance and outpatient follow-up given the benign appearance
Wound irrigation and delayed closure after 48 hours of observation
why: The classic dangerous trap - outward appearance underestimates deep tissue damage
Antibiotics alone don't address the chemical/mechanical injury needing debridement
Correct - emergency exploration within hours improves digit salvage
Delay significantly worsens outcome; this is a surgical emergency
exp: High-pressure injection injuries look deceptively benign on the surface, but injected material tracks along fascial planes causing chemical inflammation and ischemia that can lead to amputation without urgent, wide debridement - the benign initial appearance is a classic exam trap.

subject: Surgery
q: A 55-year-old man undergoing ultrasound for dyspepsia is incidentally found to have a sessile gallbladder polyp measuring 1.2 cm with no gallstones. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Statin therapy to reduce cholesterol polyp size
why: No follow-up would miss substantial malignant potential given size/age
Surveillance alone suits smaller, low-risk polyps, not this combination
Cholesterol polyps don't respond to statins for size reduction as a management strategy
Correct
exp: Gallbladder polyps over 1 cm, especially sessile, solitary, or in a patient over 50, carry significant risk of harboring or progressing to gallbladder carcinoma, so cholecystectomy is recommended; smaller low-risk polyps are followed with serial ultrasound instead.

subject: Surgery
q: A 68-year-old smoker with a lung mass presents with confusion, constipation, and polyuria. Serum calcium is elevated with a low PTH. Biopsy shows squamous cell carcinoma. What is the most likely mechanism of his hypercalcemia?
opts: Osteolytic bone metastases releasing calcium directly
Ectopic secretion of parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP)
Ectopic ACTH secretion causing Cushing syndrome
Vitamin D-mediated increased intestinal calcium absorption
why: Osteolytic hypercalcemia is more classically linked to breast cancer/myeloma with documented bone involvement, not stated here
Correct - squamous cell lung cancer is the prototypical PTHrP-secreting tumor
Ectopic ACTH Cushing syndrome is classically linked to small cell, not squamous cell, lung cancer
Vitamin D-mediated hypercalcemia is typical of lymphoma
exp: Squamous cell lung carcinoma is the classic cause of humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy via ectopic PTHrP, which mimics PTH action on bone and kidney while endogenous PTH is suppressed - mechanistically distinct from the osteolytic hypercalcemia of bone metastases.
