q: A 58-year-old man on long-term ergotamine therapy for migraines presents with dull flank and back pain, and imaging shows bilateral hydronephrosis with medial deviation of both ureters at L4-L5, without an obstructing stone. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Correct
UPJ obstruction is usually unilateral and doesn't cause medial ureteral deviation
Horseshoe kidney is a congenital anomaly present from childhood, unrelated to ergotamine
Retrocaval ureter is a congenital, typically right-sided anomaly, unrelated to drug exposure
exp: Retroperitoneal fibrosis (Ormond's disease) causes a periaortic fibro-inflammatory mass that envelops and medially deviates the ureters, causing bilateral hydronephrosis; causes include idiopathic/IgG4-related disease, ergot alkaloids, and malignancy, with management by steroids and ureterolysis if obstruction persists.

subject: Surgery
q: A 71-year-old man with prior open abdominal aortic aneurysm repair 4 years ago presents with a small self-limited episode of hematemesis followed a week later by massive gastrointestinal bleeding and hypotension. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: A bleeding ulcer doesn't classically show a herald-bleed pattern tied to prior aortic surgery
Mallory-Weiss tears follow retching/vomiting, not this history
Correct
Variceal bleeding requires underlying portal hypertension, not described here
exp: A herald bleed followed days to weeks later by massive hemorrhage in a patient with prior aortic graft surgery is classic for secondary aortoenteric fistula (graft eroding into the duodenum); it is a surgical emergency needing urgent CT angiography/endoscopy and graft excision with reconstruction.

subject: Surgery
q: A 62-year-old smoker presents with profound proximal muscle weakness, hyperpigmentation, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, and hyperglycemia over 6 weeks. Chest imaging shows a central lung mass. ACTH is markedly elevated and not suppressed by high-dose dexamethasone. What is the most likely underlying tumor?
why: Papillary thyroid carcinoma does not secrete ACTH
Bronchial carcinoids can secrete ACTH but typically cause a milder, more gradual course
An adrenal adenoma causing Cushing's would suppress, not elevate, ACTH via feedback
Correct
exp: Rapid-onset Cushing syndrome with marked hyperpigmentation, hypokalemic alkalosis, and hyperglycemia, with ACTH resistant to high-dose dexamethasone suppression, is classic for ectopic ACTH secretion from small cell lung carcinoma - its aggressive biology explains the rapid onset versus the more indolent course of ACTH-secreting carcinoids.

subject: Surgery
q: A 24-year-old woman presents with a soft, bluish, fluctuant swelling in the floor of the mouth lateral to the midline that has slowly enlarged over months, without pain or fever. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Dermoid cyst of the floor of mouth
why: Ludwig's angina is an acute, painful, rapidly progressive infection, not a slow painless swelling
Correct
Thyroglossal duct cysts are midline and move with tongue protrusion
Dermoid cysts here are typically midline and doughy, not bluish/fluctuant
exp: A ranula is a mucous extravasation cyst from the sublingual gland or its ducts, presenting as a soft, bluish, translucent floor-of-mouth swelling lateral to the midline; a plunging ranula extends through the mylohyoid into the neck, managed by marsupialization or sublingual gland excision.

subject: Surgery
q: A 50-year-old woman has an incidentally detected pancreatic tail cyst. Imaging shows a unilocular cyst with a thick wall and septations, without communication to the pancreatic duct. Intracystic CEA is markedly elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Serous cystadenomas show a honeycomb microcystic pattern and low CEA, rarely needing resection
A pseudocyst follows pancreatitis with low CEA and high amylase
Simple retention cysts are rare and don't raise CEA
Correct
exp: Mucinous cystic neoplasms typically occur in middle-aged women in the pancreatic body/tail, lack communication with the main pancreatic duct (unlike IPMN), and have elevated intracystic CEA from mucinous epithelium; resection is generally recommended given malignant potential.

subject: Surgery
q: A 70-year-old bedridden man recovering from hip fracture surgery develops massive abdominal distension. Abdominal X-ray shows a markedly dilated colon up to the splenic flexure without a transition point or mechanical obstruction on CT. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Mechanical left-sided colonic obstruction from malignancy
why: Sigmoid volvulus shows a characteristic coffee bean sign with a twisted loop, not diffuse dilation
Toxic megacolon occurs with fulminant colitis and systemic toxicity, not described here
Correct
CT here explicitly excludes a mechanical transition point or mass
exp: Ogilvie syndrome is acute massive colonic dilation without mechanical obstruction, classically in elderly, immobile, or postoperative patients; management is conservative (correct electrolytes, decompression) with IV neostigmine or colonoscopic decompression if cecal diameter exceeds 12 cm, to prevent perforation.

subject: Surgery
q: A 19-year-old thin young woman presents with left flank pain and intermittent hematuria, worse on standing. CT angiography shows compression of the left renal vein between the superior mesenteric artery and the aorta with dilation proximal to the compression. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Renal artery stenosis from fibromuscular dysplasia
why: FMD causes a string of beads renal artery appearance with hypertension, not venous compression
Renal vein thrombosis would show a filling defect, not mechanical compression with proximal dilation
Posterior nutcracker refers to a variant compressed behind the aorta, not the anterior compression described
Correct
exp: Nutcracker syndrome results from compression of the left renal vein between the SMA and aorta, causing venous hypertension in the left kidney with hematuria and flank pain in young, thin patients; management ranges from observation to renal vein stenting or surgical transposition in severe cases.

subject: Surgery
q: A 45-year-old woman presents with the sudden onset of the worst headache of her life, vomiting, and neck stiffness, with no history of trauma. Non-contrast CT head performed within 6 hours is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Reassure and discharge since CT excludes hemorrhage
MRI brain with contrast as the next investigation
why: CT sensitivity, though high early, is not 100 percent; discharging risks missing a leaking aneurysm
Correct
Antiepileptics are not the immediate diagnostic step for suspected SAH
MRI is not the standard next step; LP is more immediately informative
exp: Sudden severe thunderclap headache suggests aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage; while non-contrast CT within 6 hours has very high sensitivity, it is not absolute, so a normal early CT with high clinical suspicion warrants lumbar puncture for xanthochromia before further vascular imaging.

subject: Surgery
q: A 55-year-old man presents with a palpable firm neck mass, serum calcium of 15.8 mg/dL, and PTH ten times the upper limit of normal. What is the most appropriate initial management?
opts: En bloc surgical resection without preoperative FNAC
FNAC of the neck mass to confirm diagnosis before surgery
Minimally invasive parathyroidectomy with intraoperative PTH monitoring only
why: Correct
FNAC risks seeding a potentially malignant parathyroid tumor and is avoided when carcinoma is suspected
Cinacalcet controls hypercalcemia medically but is not curative for carcinoma
Minimally invasive parathyroidectomy suits benign single-gland adenomas, not suspected carcinoma
exp: A palpable neck mass with markedly elevated calcium and PTH should raise suspicion for parathyroid carcinoma rather than a typical adenoma; en bloc resection without prior FNAC or capsule violation is recommended, since biopsy risks tumor seeding along the needle tract.

subject: Surgery
q: A 60-year-old man presents with a non-healing, indurated, ulcerated lesion with rolled everted edges arising within a 30-year-old burn scar on his forearm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Marjolin's ulcer (squamous cell carcinoma in a chronic scar)
Basal cell carcinoma arising de novo
why: A simple infected scar would improve with antibiotics/wound care, not progressively ulcerate with rolled edges
Keloid degeneration is not a recognized malignant transformation pathway
Correct
Marjolin's ulcers are overwhelmingly squamous cell carcinoma, not basal cell, given the chronic scar origin
exp: Marjolin's ulcer is a squamous cell carcinoma arising in a chronic wound, burn scar, or sinus tract, typically after a long latency; any non-healing or changing ulcer within an old scar should be biopsied to exclude malignant transformation, and treatment is wide local excision.

subject: Surgery
q: A 30-year-old man involved in a road traffic accident with a pelvic fracture and gross hematuria undergoes a retrograde cystogram, which shows contrast extravasation confined around the bladder base without entering the peritoneal cavity. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Immediate exploratory laparotomy and bladder repair
Prolonged Foley catheter drainage with conservative management
why: Surgical repair is reserved for intraperitoneal rupture, which needs closure due to peritonitis risk.
Addresses upper tract obstruction, irrelevant to a bladder injury.
Some catheter drainage is still required to keep the bladder decompressed and allow healing.
Correct - extraperitoneal bladder rupture is managed conservatively with prolonged catheter drainage.
exp: Extraperitoneal bladder rupture, the more common pattern with pelvic fracture, is managed conservatively with prolonged (10-14 day) Foley catheter drainage in most cases, reserving surgery for concomitant injuries, bone fragments in the bladder wall, or failure to heal.

subject: Surgery
q: A 68-year-old man had a transient episode of right-sided weakness and slurred speech lasting 20 minutes last week, and carotid Doppler now shows 75% stenosis of the left internal carotid artery. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Carotid artery stenting only if stenosis reaches 100%
why: Correct - endarterectomy reduces stroke risk in symptomatic, high-grade (>=70%) stenosis.
Background medical management does not substitute for revascularization at this symptomatic, high-grade stenosis.
Waiting for complete occlusion forfeits the window for benefit; near-total occlusion is often not amenable to surgery.
Not indicated for atherosclerotic carotid stenosis, which is not a cardioembolic source.
exp: In a symptomatic patient (recent TIA/stroke referable to the carotid territory) with high-grade (>=70%) ipsilateral carotid stenosis, carotid endarterectomy - ideally within 2 weeks of the event, in a low-surgical-risk patient - significantly reduces stroke risk compared with medical therapy alone, per NASCET trial evidence.

subject: Surgery
q: During right thyroid lobectomy, the recurrent laryngeal nerve is not found in its expected tracheoesophageal groove course; instead a nerve enters the larynx directly off the vagus at a near-horizontal course high in the neck. Preoperative imaging had shown an aberrant right subclavian artery arising distal to the left subclavian. What should the surgeon anticipate?
opts: Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy is imminent
A non-recurrent laryngeal nerve, arising directly from the vagus without looping around the subclavian artery
An anomalous superior laryngeal nerve replacing the RLN entirely
The nerve seen is the ansa cervicalis and can be safely divided
why: The finding described is anatomical variance, not evidence of imminent bilateral injury.
Correct - a non-recurrent laryngeal nerve is strongly linked to an aberrant right subclavian artery, since the vessel it would otherwise loop around never forms.
The superior laryngeal nerve is a separate branch that does not replace RLN function.
The ansa cervicalis is a strap-muscle motor loop unrelated to laryngeal innervation; dividing the nerve seen here would cause vocal cord palsy.
exp: A non-recurrent laryngeal nerve occurs almost exclusively on the right side and is strongly associated with an aberrant right subclavian artery (arising distal to the left subclavian, crossing behind the oesophagus) - because the fourth arch-derived right subclavian never forms, the nerve never needs to "recur" around it. Preoperative vascular imaging findings should prompt anticipation of this variant to avoid injuring it intraoperatively.

subject: Surgery
q: A 65-year-old male smoker presents with a slow-growing, soft, non-tender mass in the tail of the parotid gland; imaging suggests a cystic lesion, and a similar smaller nodule is noted in the contralateral parotid. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: The most common parotid tumour overall but usually solid and unilateral, without this smoking/bilaterality link.
The commonest malignant salivary tumour, usually a firmer, potentially fixed mass, not this benign cystic bilateral picture.
Correct - older male smokers, parotid tail, cystic, bilateral/multifocal in a meaningful minority.
Presents acutely with pain, fever and erythema, not a slow-growing painless course.
exp: Warthin's tumour classically occurs in older male smokers, arises in the tail of the parotid, is often cystic on imaging, and is bilateral/multifocal in a meaningful minority of cases - distinguishing it from the far more common pleomorphic adenoma.

subject: Surgery
q: An asymptomatic 70-year-old woman is found incidentally to have circumferential calcification of the gallbladder wall on an abdominal CT done for an unrelated reason. What is the most appropriate management?
why: Ignores the recognized malignancy association of a porcelain gallbladder.
Used for cholesterol gallstone dissolution/prevention, not relevant to a calcified wall.
Does not address the standing cancer risk in a fit surgical candidate.
Correct - porcelain gallbladder carries increased gallbladder carcinoma risk, favoring prophylactic surgery.
exp: A porcelain gallbladder - dystrophic calcification of the gallbladder wall, usually from chronic cholecystitis - carries an increased risk of gallbladder carcinoma; current teaching favors prophylactic cholecystectomy in a surgically fit patient.

subject: Surgery
q: A patient with large bowel obstruction and a competent ileocecal valve is found on CT to have a closed-loop obstruction with the cecum measuring 13 cm in diameter. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Urgent surgical intervention because of impending perforation
Trial of nasogastric decompression and observation for 48 hours
why: Correct - by Laplace's law, this closed-loop cecal distension carries high perforation risk and needs urgent surgery.
Does not relieve a closed-loop obstruction and risks perforation while waiting.
Far too delayed for an actively distending, high-risk cecum.
Bowel-stimulating measures are contraindicated in obstruction and add perforation risk.
exp: By Laplace's law, wall tension rises with radius, so a distended, closed-loop-obstructed cecum is at high risk of ischemia/perforation once diameter exceeds roughly 9-12 cm; 13 cm in a closed loop is a surgical emergency, not something to observe.

subject: Surgery
q: A 32-year-old woman with no cardiovascular risk factors presents with new-onset severe hypertension. CT angiography shows a 'string of beads' appearance of the mid-to-distal right renal artery. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Occurs in older patients with vascular risk factors and affects the proximal/ostial artery, not this age/pattern.
Correct - young women, mid-to-distal artery, classic string-of-beads appearance, a correctable hypertension cause.
Presents with flank pain, hematuria and nephrotic-range proteinuria, not this angiographic finding.
Causes a smooth, not beaded, large-vessel stenosis with raised inflammatory markers and aortic involvement.
exp: Fibromuscular dysplasia typically affects young women, involves the mid-to-distal renal artery, and produces the classic 'string of beads' angiographic appearance from alternating stenosis and aneurysmal dilation; it is a correctable cause of secondary hypertension, often responsive to angioplasty.

subject: Surgery
q: A 50-year-old man with a known pituitary macroadenoma develops sudden severe headache, vomiting, diplopia and reduced consciousness over a few hours. MRI shows hemorrhage within the pituitary tumour. What is the diagnosis?
why: MRI/CT would show subarachnoid, not intratumoural, blood in a known adenoma.
Typically has a more insidious course over days-weeks after minor trauma in the elderly, not this acute picture.
Correct - sudden hemorrhage into a pituitary adenoma with headache, ophthalmoplegia and reduced consciousness.
Presents with proptosis, chemosis and multiple cranial nerve palsies without necessarily an intratumoural bleed.
exp: Pituitary apoplexy is sudden hemorrhage or infarction within a pituitary adenoma, presenting with abrupt severe headache, visual field/cranial nerve deficits and potential acute hypopituitarism - a neurosurgical/endocrine emergency requiring urgent stress-dose steroids and consideration of decompressive surgery.

subject: Surgery
q: A patient has biochemically confirmed excess catecholamine production with markedly elevated plasma metanephrines, but CT of the adrenals is normal. What is the best next investigation to localize the tumour?
opts: Fine needle aspiration of the adrenal glands
why: Repeating the same biochemical test does not help localize the tumour.
Has poor sensitivity for extra-adrenal/small paragangliomas compared with functional imaging.
Contraindicated for a suspected pheochromocytoma, risking a hypertensive crisis, and irrelevant when CT is normal.
Correct - MIBG scintigraphy localizes catecholamine-secreting tissue including extra-adrenal sites.
exp: When biochemistry confirms a catecholamine-secreting tumour but adrenal imaging is negative, extra-adrenal disease (paraganglioma) must be sought; 123I-MIBG scintigraphy (or functional PET where available) localizes catecholamine-secreting tissue throughout the body, including extra-adrenal and metastatic sites.

q: A patient with 45% total body surface area burns develops hematemesis and melena on day 4 of admission despite hemodynamic stability. Endoscopy shows diffuse gastric and duodenal mucosal erosions. What is the diagnosis and the key preventive measure that was likely omitted?
opts: Curling's ulcer; stress ulcer prophylaxis was not given
Mallory-Weiss tear; antiemetics were not given
Variceal bleed; beta-blocker prophylaxis was not given
Boerhaave syndrome; a nasogastric tube was not placed
why: Correct - diffuse stress-related gastroduodenal erosions in a major burn define Curling's ulcer, preventable with prophylaxis.
A Mallory-Weiss tear follows forceful retching, producing a longitudinal tear, not diffuse erosions, and is unrelated to burns.
Requires underlying portal hypertension/liver disease, not indicated here.
A full-thickness esophageal rupture presenting with chest pain/mediastinitis, not diffuse gastric erosions.
exp: Curling's ulcer is a stress-related diffuse gastroduodenal mucosal erosion/ulceration classically associated with major burns, related to mucosal ischemia from burn shock and increased gastric acid; routine stress ulcer prophylaxis alongside early enteral feeding in major burns is standard specifically to prevent this complication.

subject: Surgery
q: A 28-year-old woman on long-term combined oral contraceptives presents with sudden severe right upper quadrant pain and hypotension; CT shows a large hemorrhagic liver mass with hemoperitoneum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Also more common in women but not typically OCP-driven, has a central scar, and rupture/hemorrhage is rare.
Correct - hepatic adenomas are OCP-associated and prone to spontaneous hemorrhage/rupture.
Classically occurs on a background of cirrhosis/chronic liver disease in an older patient, not this demographic.
The most common benign liver tumour but rupture is exceedingly rare even when large, with no OCP link.
exp: Hepatic adenomas are strongly associated with long-term oral contraceptive/anabolic steroid use, are prone to spontaneous hemorrhage/rupture (especially when >5 cm), and can present as an acute abdomen with hemoperitoneum; management includes stopping the OCP and resection for large, symptomatic or ruptured lesions.

q: A 30-year-old man after blunt chest trauma has hypotension, distended neck veins, and muffled heart sounds. On checking blood pressure, systolic pressure falls by 15 mmHg during inspiration. What is this finding called and what is its mechanism?
opts: Kussmaul's sign; paradoxical rise in JVP on inspiration from impaired RV filling
Pulsus alternans; alternating strong-weak pulse from LV dysfunction
Pulsus bisferiens; double-peaked pulse from combined AR and HOCM
Pulsus paradoxus; exaggerated inspiratory fall in systolic BP from septal shift limiting LV filling in a non-compliant pericardial sac
why: Kussmaul's sign is a paradoxical rise in JVP on inspiration, a different (though related) sign
Pulsus alternans reflects severe LV systolic dysfunction, unrelated to respiration
Pulsus bisferiens is a double-peaked pulse from combined valvular lesions
Correct — inspiration increases RV venous return, bulging the septum leftward and reducing LV filling in the tense pericardial sac
exp: Pulsus paradoxus (inspiratory systolic fall greater than 10 mmHg) occurs in tamponade from septal shift limiting LV filling within a tense, fluid-filled pericardium.

q: A 55-year-old woman with long-standing primary hyperparathyroidism (pre-op calcium 13.2 mg/dL, large adenoma, radiological bone changes) undergoes parathyroidectomy. On post-op day 2 she develops severe symptomatic hypocalcemia (corrected calcium 6.8 mg/dL) needing large, prolonged IV calcium infusions, with associated hypophosphatemia and hypomagnesemia. What is this phenomenon called?
opts: Post-surgical hypoparathyroidism from inadvertent gland removal
why: Correct — demineralized bone rapidly re-uptakes calcium and phosphate after correcting severe, long-standing PHPT
Hypoparathyroidism from gland injury is usually milder/transient and lacks the marked hypophosphatemia seen here
DiGeorge is a congenital cause of hypoparathyroidism, irrelevant here
Milk-alkali causes hypercalcemia, the opposite picture
exp: Hungry bone syndrome follows correction of long-standing severe hyperparathyroidism, causing profound, prolonged hypocalcemia with hypophosphatemia and hypomagnesemia.

q: A 35-year-old man sustains flame burns to his entire right upper limb (front and back) and the anterior trunk. Using the Rule of Nines, what is the estimated TBSA burned?
why: 18% is anterior trunk alone, missing the limb
Correct — whole limb (9%) plus anterior trunk (18%) equals 27%
9% is one upper limb alone
36% overestimates the area described
exp: Rule of Nines: each whole upper limb is 9%, anterior trunk is 18%. Total here is 9 plus 18 equals 27%.

q: A 78-year-old man on warfarin has 3 weeks of worsening headache, gait unsteadiness, and mild confusion, after recalling a minor fall 3 weeks ago. CT head shows a crescent-shaped, hypodense extra-axial collection crossing suture lines with midline shift. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: EDH is lentiform, limited by suture lines, and presents acutely with a lucid interval, not over weeks
Acute SDH would be hyperdense and present within hours to days, not 3 weeks
Correct — a crescentic, hypodense collection crossing suture lines in an elderly/anticoagulated patient weeks after trauma
SAH presents with thunderclap headache and blood in the sulci/cisterns, not a crescentic extra-axial collection
exp: Chronic subdural hematoma classically appears in elderly/anticoagulated patients weeks after minor trauma, with insidious headache, confusion, and gait disturbance.

q: A 55-year-old woman has fever with chills, right upper quadrant pain, and jaundice, with no hypotension or altered mental status. Ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct with choledocholithiasis. What is this triad called, and what is it diagnostic of?
why: Reynolds pentad needs the two additional features (hypotension, confusion), absent here
Courvoisier's law refers to a palpable, non-tender gallbladder with painless jaundice suggesting malignancy, a different concept
Boas' sign is referred hyperesthesia below the right scapula in cholecystitis
Correct — fever/chills, RUQ pain, and jaundice make up Charcot's triad of acute cholangitis
exp: Charcot's triad (fever/chills, RUQ pain, jaundice) is the classic presentation of acute cholangitis; adding hypotension and confusion (Reynolds pentad) signals suppurative progression.

q: A newborn boy has the urethral meatus opening on the ventral penile shaft with ventral curvature (chordee) on erection, and an incomplete, hooded foreskin. What is the most important immediate counselling point for the parents?
opts: This is hypospadias; circumcision should be avoided as the foreskin will be needed for later surgical repair
Circumcision should be performed immediately for religious/cultural reasons
This requires emergency surgery within 24 hours
This is a normal variant requiring no follow-up
why: Correct — the hooded prepuce provides tissue for later urethroplasty
Circumcision discards tissue needed for the repair
Surgery is elective/delayed for optimal outcomes, not an emergency
This is a structural anomaly requiring urology referral, not simple observation
exp: In hypospadias, the hooded ventral prepuce is used as tissue for reconstructive urethroplasty, so circumcision must be avoided; repair is typically elective around 6-18 months.

subject: Surgery
q: A 68-year-old man has an asymptomatic infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm of 5.8 cm on screening ultrasound, with no symptoms of rupture. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Observation with repeat ultrasound in 12 months
why: Observation suits AAA below the intervention threshold, not 5.8cm
Correct — elective repair is indicated for AAA at or above 5.5cm in men
Emergency laparotomy is for ruptured/symptomatic AAA, not an asymptomatic finding
Medical therapy is adjunctive, not a substitute for repair once the threshold is met
exp: Elective repair (open or EVAR) is indicated for an asymptomatic AAA at or above 5.5cm in men, or one growing more than 1cm/year, since rupture risk rises steeply beyond this threshold.

subject: Surgery
q: A 62-year-old man is diagnosed with pancreatic adenocarcinoma and undergoes a Whipple procedure. Which serum tumor marker is most useful for post-operative surveillance, keeping in mind it can be falsely elevated by biliary obstruction?
why: CEA is a colorectal marker, only modestly useful here
AFP is used for HCC/germ cell tumours
Correct — CA 19-9 is standard for pancreatic adenocarcinoma prognostication/surveillance, but cholestasis can falsely elevate it
CA 125 is primarily an ovarian cancer marker
exp: CA 19-9 is the standard marker for pancreatic adenocarcinoma surveillance, but biliary obstruction can falsely elevate it, and about 10% of patients are Lewis-antigen negative and never express it.

q: A 25-year-old factory worker has a clean guillotine amputation of the index finger at the proximal phalanx. The amputated part was wrapped in dry gauze and placed in direct contact with ice (not in a sealed bag) during a 14-hour transport. What is the most likely reason replantation may now fail?
opts: Warm ischemia time exceeded acceptable limits
Guillotine-type amputations are never suitable for replantation
14 hours exceeds the absolute time limit for digit replantation regardless of cooling
Improper cooling technique caused direct tissue freezing/frostbite injury to the part
why: No warm-ischemia interval is described here — the part was cooled from the time of amputation, so warm ischemia is not the issue
Clean guillotine amputations are actually favourable for replantation compared with avulsion
Digits can tolerate cold ischemia well beyond 14 hours if properly cooled, so time alone is not the limiting factor
Correct — direct ice contact without a protective sealed bag causes frostbite/crystal damage to the part
exp: The amputated part should be wrapped in saline-moistened gauze, sealed in a plastic bag, and only then placed on ice; direct ice contact can cause frostbite damage even within an acceptable ischemia window.

subject: Surgery
q: Before a right hepatectomy for a tumor confined to the right lobe, the surgeon reviews Couinaud segmental anatomy. Which segments constitute the anatomical right lobe (right hepatectomy specimen) as divided by Cantlie's line?
why: Correct — these are the functional right-lobe segments divided by Cantlie's line
These are the left-lobe segments
This mixes part of the left lobe with the caudate, not the right lobe
VI and VII are only the posterior right segments, excluding V and VIII
exp: Cantlie's line divides the liver into functional right (segments V, VI, VII, VIII) and left (II, III, IVa, IVb) lobes, independent of the anatomical falciform-ligament division.

subject: Surgery
q: A 60-year-old man has a rectal adenocarcinoma 2 cm from the anal verge, with imaging showing invasion into the external anal sphincter complex. Which procedure is most appropriate?
opts: Low anterior resection (LAR) with colorectal anastomosis
why: LAR needs an adequate distal margin and sphincter preservation, not feasible with sphincter invasion this low
Correct — sphincter invasion this low mandates APR with a permanent end colostomy
Local excision suits only early, small, favourable-histology tumours without sphincter involvement
Total colectomy is for diffuse colonic disease, not an isolated low rectal cancer
exp: A tumor this low with sphincter-complex invasion cannot achieve an adequate distal margin or preserve continence, mandating APR over a sphincter-sparing approach.

subject: Surgery
q: A 58-year-old man presents with epigastric pain and unintentional weight loss of 6 kg over 3 months. Upper GI endoscopy shows a 2 cm elevated gastric lesion. Endoscopic ultrasound confirms the tumor is confined to the mucosa and submucosa, with no nodal enlargement on staging CT. Which statement correctly classifies this lesion?
opts: This qualifies as "early gastric cancer," a definition based on depth of invasion (mucosa/submucosa) irrespective of lymph node status
This cannot be called early gastric cancer unless the tumor is also under 2 cm in size
This cannot be called early gastric cancer unless imaging confirms absence of nodal metastasis
This cannot be called early gastric cancer unless histology shows well-differentiated cells
why: Correct: early gastric cancer is defined purely by depth of invasion, regardless of size, nodal status, or grade
Size is not part of the definition of early gastric cancer
Nodal status, even if positive, does not exclude the diagnosis of early gastric cancer
Differentiation grade is not part of the depth-based definition
exp: Early gastric cancer (EGC) is defined by the Japanese Gastric Cancer Association as tumor invasion limited to the mucosa or submucosa, regardless of tumor size, differentiation, or lymph node status; roughly 5-20% of EGC already have nodal micrometastases, so nodal positivity does not exclude the diagnosis.

subject: Surgery
q: A 45-year-old woman with recurrent Proteus mirabilis urinary infections presents with dull flank pain. Non-contrast CT KUB shows a large branched calculus filling the renal pelvis and extending into the calyces; urine pH is 8.2. What is the stone composition and best management?
opts: Calcium oxalate stone; treat with ESWL alone
Struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) stone; treat with percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL)
Uric acid stone; treat with urinary alkalinization
why: Calcium oxalate stones are usually smaller, radio-opaque and non-branching, and form in acidic/normal urine, not this alkaline-urine staghorn presentation
Correct: alkaline urine, a urease-producing organism, and a staghorn morphology together are classic for struvite stones, best cleared with PCNL
Uric acid stones are radiolucent and form in persistently acidic urine, unrelated to urease-producing organisms
Cystine stones occur in cystinuria and show hexagonal crystals on microscopy, a distinct clinical entity
exp: A branching staghorn calculus with alkaline urine and a urease-producing organism (Proteus, Klebsiella) is a struvite stone; PCNL is preferred over ESWL for staghorn calculi because it achieves more complete single-session clearance, essential since residual fragments perpetuate infection.

subject: Surgery
q: A 40-year-old man has long-standing great saphenous varicosities with medial gaiter-area pigmentation. On the multiple (staged) tourniquet test, a tourniquet applied at mid-thigh fails to control filling of the varicosities below it, though filling above the tourniquet is controlled. What does this localize?
opts: The sapheno-femoral junction alone is incompetent
An incompetent perforator exists below the level of the mid-thigh tourniquet
The tourniquet test cannot be used to localize perforator incompetence
why: If the SFJ alone were responsible, a high (groin-level) tourniquet would control all filling, which is not what is described here
The sapheno-popliteal junction is assessed with a tourniquet placed in the popliteal fossa, not relevant to this mid-thigh finding
Correct: failure to control filling below a given tourniquet level localizes an incompetent perforator below that level
This is precisely the historical and still-tested purpose of the staged tourniquet test
exp: The multiple (staged) tourniquet test localizes the level of an incompetent perforator: continued filling below a tourniquet despite control above it means a perforator below that tourniquet level is incompetent, distinct from sapheno-femoral or sapheno-popliteal junction incompetence.

subject: Surgery
q: A 52-year-old woman has a 3.5 cm invasive ductal carcinoma of the left breast. Two mobile ipsilateral axillary lymph nodes are palpable and FNAC-confirmed as metastatic. Staging workup shows no distant disease. What is the TNM stage?
why: Incorrect N-stage: nodes are histologically positive here, not N0
T3 requires a tumor greater than 5 cm, which this 3.5 cm tumor is not
N2 requires 4-9 involved nodes or matted/fixed nodes, not met with only two mobile nodes
Correct: T2 (2-5 cm) + N1 (1-3 ipsilateral nodes) + M0 stages as IIB
exp: AJCC 8th edition: T2 covers tumors 2-5 cm, N1 covers 1-3 ipsilateral axillary nodes, and this combination with M0 stages as IIB - a commonly tested TNM-to-stage conversion.

q: A 22-year-old woman develops a raised, red, itchy scar 6 weeks after ear piercing. The scar remains confined to the original wound margins and begins to flatten spontaneously over the following months. What feature identifies this as a hypertrophic scar rather than a keloid?
opts: Its confinement within the original wound margins with spontaneous regression over time
The presence of itching and erythema
Its onset within weeks of the injury
why: Correct: staying within wound boundaries and regressing spontaneously over months to years is the defining hypertrophic-scar behavior, unlike a keloid which extends beyond the wound and persists or enlarges
Itching and erythema occur in both hypertrophic scars and keloids and do not discriminate between them
Both entities can begin within weeks of injury; onset timing alone is not discriminatory
The earlobe is actually a classic keloid-prone site, so location alone would favor keloid, not hypertrophic scar
exp: The reliable bedside distinction between a hypertrophic scar and a keloid is behavioral: a hypertrophic scar stays within the original wound margins and regresses spontaneously over months to a couple of years, whereas a keloid extends beyond the wound margins, keeps growing, and rarely regresses without treatment.

subject: Surgery
q: A 55-year-old man with Child-Pugh A hepatitis B-related cirrhosis is asymptomatic. What is the recommended surveillance protocol for early detection of hepatocellular carcinoma?
opts: Ultrasound abdomen, with or without serum AFP, every 6 months
why: An annual interval is too infrequent for a tumor that can double in months, and CT carries unnecessary radiation/contrast burden for routine surveillance
Correct: 6-monthly abdominal ultrasound, with or without AFP, is the recommended surveillance tool and interval in cirrhotic patients
AFP alone has poor sensitivity and specificity and is not used as a stand-alone surveillance test
MRI every 3 months is neither the recommended modality nor interval for routine surveillance; it is reserved for characterizing indeterminate nodules found on ultrasound
exp: Cirrhotic patients require HCC surveillance with abdominal ultrasound (plus or minus AFP) every 6 months; CT or MRI is reserved for characterizing a nodule already found on ultrasound, not as the first-line periodic surveillance test.

q: A 68-year-old man presents with left iliac fossa pain, fever, and a tender palpable mass. CT abdomen shows sigmoid diverticulitis with a 4 cm abscess walled off close to the colon by adjacent bowel loops, with no free perforation or diffuse peritonitis. What is the Hinchey stage and appropriate initial management?
opts: Hinchey III; requires emergency Hartmann's procedure
Hinchey IV; requires laparotomy with peritoneal lavage
Hinchey I; percutaneous drainage plus IV antibiotics is indicated for an abscess of this size (4 cm or larger), otherwise antibiotics alone suffice
Hinchey II; requires immediate laparotomy regardless of abscess size
why: Hinchey III describes purulent peritonitis from a ruptured abscess, not this contained pericolic collection
Hinchey IV describes feculent peritonitis from free perforation, which is not present here
Correct: a pericolic abscess close to the colon is Hinchey I, and abscesses around 4 cm or larger warrant percutaneous drainage alongside antibiotics
This mislabels the stage as II, which describes a distant/pelvic abscess, and overstates the need for immediate surgery
exp: Hinchey I is a localized pericolic or mesenteric abscess; abscesses of roughly 4 cm or larger are generally drained percutaneously under image guidance with concurrent IV antibiotics, while smaller collections often respond to antibiotics alone. Surgery is reserved for higher Hinchey stages or failure of conservative management.

subject: Surgery
q: A 35-year-old man with a neglected carious lower molar develops rapidly progressive bilateral submandibular and sublingual swelling, tongue elevation, drooling, and stridor over 24 hours. What is the most urgent priority in management?
opts: Start intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics and reassess in 6 hours before any other step
Obtain a contrast CT neck to confirm the diagnosis before intervening
Proceed directly to incision and drainage of the submandibular space under general anesthesia
Secure the airway first, using awake fibre-optic intubation or tracheostomy if intubation fails, before other measures
why: Antibiotics are essential but do not address an airway that is imminently at risk of obstruction
Imaging must never delay management of a threatened airway in this setting
Inducing general anesthesia before securing a difficult, distorted airway risks complete airway loss
Correct: the airway must be secured first given the risk of rapid obstruction from tongue elevation and floor-of-mouth swelling
exp: Ludwig's angina is a rapidly spreading bilateral cellulitis of the submandibular, sublingual and submental spaces that elevates and displaces the tongue, threatening airway obstruction; the airway must be secured first (awake fibre-optic intubation preferred, tracheostomy as backup) before antibiotics, imaging, or surgical drainage.

subject: Surgery
q: A 60-year-old man with CKD stage 5 on hemodialysis had a radiocephalic (Brescia-Cimino) arteriovenous fistula created at the wrist. At 6 weeks, examination reveals a continuous low-pitched thrill and bruit over the fistula, with a soft, easily compressible pulse that augments on proximal occlusion. What does this indicate?
opts: Successful fistula maturation; the fistula is now suitable for cannulation
Fistula failure requiring immediate surgical revision
Steal syndrome, requiring banding of the fistula
why: Correct: a continuous low-pitched machinery bruit and thrill, with a soft compressible augmenting pulse, reflect high continuous flow through the fistula, the hallmark of successful maturation and readiness for cannulation
Failure or thrombosis presents with an absent thrill and a weak or absent pulse, not this pattern
Steal syndrome presents with distal limb ischemia (coldness, pain, pallor of the hand), not simply a thrill
Venous hypertension presents with limb swelling and dilated collateral veins, not an isolated thrill or pulse finding
exp: A matured arteriovenous fistula ready for cannulation is confirmed by a continuous thrill and bruit plus a soft, compressible, augmenting pulse; the commonly cited Rule of 6s is flow greater than 600 mL/min, vein diameter greater than 6 mm, and depth less than 6 mm from skin, typically achieved by around 6 weeks. A bounding water-hammer pulse, by contrast, signals outflow venous stenosis rather than healthy maturation.

q: A 50-year-old woman has a long-standing multinodular goitre. She now reports progressive dysphagia and positional dyspnea. CT shows tracheal deviation with the airway narrowed to 60% of normal caliber, and retrosternal extension of the goitre. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Continue observation with annual ultrasound follow-up
why: Observation is inappropriate once compressive and airway symptoms are already present
Correct: compressive symptoms with confirmed tracheal narrowing and retrosternal extension are absolute indications for surgery, irrespective of thyroid function
Radioactive iodine is not first-line for a large compressive goitre and can transiently worsen swelling and airway compromise, especially with retrosternal extension
Suppression therapy is ineffective for established long-standing nodular disease and does not relieve mechanical compression
exp: Compressive symptoms (dysphagia, positional dyspnea) together with radiologically confirmed tracheal narrowing and retrosternal extension are absolute indications for surgery in multinodular goitre; total thyroidectomy is preferred over subtotal resection to avoid recurrence.

subject: Surgery
q: A 30-year-old kitchen worker presents with 3 days of throbbing pain and swelling along the lateral nail fold of the right index finger, with visible pus beneath the eponychium. The pulp of the fingertip is normal and non-tender. What is the diagnosis and first-line treatment?
opts: Felon; requires a longitudinal incision over the pulp for drainage
Herpetic whitlow; treat with acyclovir and avoid incision
Paronychia; requires incision and drainage of the nail fold, with partial or complete nail plate removal if there is subungual extension
Suppurative flexor tenosynovitis; requires assessment for Kanavel's signs and urgent surgical drainage
why: Felon involves the fingertip pulp pad and is drained via a pulp incision, but the pulp here is explicitly normal, ruling this out
Herpetic whitlow presents with grouped vesicles rather than frank pus, and incision is contraindicated since it is a viral infection
Correct: paronychia is infection of the nail fold, treated by draining the fold with nail plate removal if pus has tracked beneath it
Flexor tenosynovitis shows Kanavel's signs (fusiform swelling, flexed posture, sheath tenderness, pain on passive extension), none of which are described here
exp: Paronychia is a bacterial infection confined to the nail fold (lateral and/or eponychial), managed by incision and drainage of the fold with partial or total nail plate removal if pus has tracked subungually; a normal, non-tender pulp distinguishes it from felon.

q: A 42-year-old woman presents with progressive headache and difficulty seeing objects in her peripheral vision on both sides, causing her to bump into door frames. MRI shows a 2.5 cm pituitary macroadenoma with suprasellar extension compressing the optic chiasm. Which visual field defect is classically produced?
opts: Homonymous hemianopia, from compression of the optic tract
Monocular blindness, from compression of one optic nerve
Central scotoma, from compression of the macular fibers
Bitemporal hemianopia, from compression of the decussating nasal retinal fibers at the chiasm
why: Homonymous hemianopia results from a lesion posterior to the chiasm such as the optic tract, radiation, or occipital cortex, not a midline chiasmal lesion
Monocular blindness suggests a prechiasmal (optic nerve) lesion rather than chiasmal compression
Central scotoma suggests macular or optic nerve pathology such as optic neuritis, not chiasmal compression
Correct: compression from below at the chiasm affects the decussating nasal-retinal fibers first, producing bitemporal hemianopia
exp: A pituitary macroadenoma compresses the optic chiasm from below, first affecting the decussating fibers arising from the nasal retina of each eye (which carry the temporal visual fields), producing the classic bitemporal hemianopia of chiasmal compression.

subject: Surgery
q: An 80-year-old multiparous woman presents with a mass protruding from the anus on straining that reduces spontaneously, along with mucus discharge and mild fecal incontinence. On examination, the protruding mass shows concentric circular mucosal folds and measures 6 cm beyond the anal verge. What is the diagnosis, and what distinguishes it from prolapsed hemorrhoids?
opts: Complete (full-thickness) rectal prolapse; the concentric circular mucosal folds distinguish it from the radial grooves seen in prolapsed hemorrhoids
Prolapsed hemorrhoids; the radial mucosal folds seen here confirm the diagnosis
Rectal polyp; the finding of a solitary pedunculated mass confirms the diagnosis
Anal fissure with sentinel pile; a longitudinal fissure confirms the diagnosis
why: Correct: concentric circular mucosal folds are the defining feature that distinguishes full-thickness rectal prolapse from prolapsed hemorrhoids
This describes hemorrhoids' own feature (radial, not concentric folds), which is not what is seen in this vignette
A polyp is a discrete pedunculated lesion, not a diffuse circumferential prolapse as described
Fissures present with pain and a linear tear, not a protruding circumferential mass
exp: On inspection, full-thickness rectal prolapse (procidentia) shows concentric circular mucosal folds, while prolapsed hemorrhoids show radial furrows or grooves between individual piles - this is the key bedside sign separating the two conditions.

subject: Surgery
q: A sexually active young man in his mid-20s presents with gradual-onset scrotal pain and swelling over 2 days, fever, and dysuria. Elevating the scrotum relieves the pain, and the cremasteric reflex is intact. What is the most likely diagnosis and the clinical sign supporting it?
opts: Testicular torsion; Prehn's sign is positive because pain worsens on elevation
Epididymo-orchitis; Prehn's sign is positive because pain is relieved on elevation
Testicular torsion; the absent cremasteric reflex confirms the diagnosis
Torsion of the appendix testis; the blue dot sign confirms the diagnosis
why: This describes torsion's classical sudden-onset, non-relieved presentation, which does not match this case
Correct: gradual onset, fever, dysuria, an intact cremasteric reflex, and pain relief on elevation together favor epididymo-orchitis
An absent cremasteric reflex is a torsion feature and is explicitly not present in this vignette, where the reflex is intact
Appendix testis torsion typically occurs in prepubertal boys with a tender nodule and blue dot sign at the upper testicular pole, not this presentation
exp: Gradual onset with fever and dysuria (suggesting a urinary source), an intact cremasteric reflex, and relief of pain on scrotal elevation (positive Prehn's sign) together favor epididymo-orchitis over torsion; note that Prehn's sign has limited sensitivity and specificity in current literature and should never delay urgent Doppler ultrasound when torsion is genuinely suspected.

subject: Surgery
q: A 10-year-old boy with a supracondylar humerus fracture in a tight cast develops severe forearm pain out of proportion to injury, pallor, and pain on passive finger extension 6 hours after casting, with a feeble radial pulse. The most appropriate immediate step is to:
opts: Elevate the limb and reassess in 2 hours
Obtain a Doppler arterial study before any intervention
Split/remove the cast completely and proceed to emergency fasciotomy if signs persist
Start IV analgesics and observe overnight
why: Delay risks irreversible ischemic damage
Compartment syndrome is a clinical diagnosis; waiting for imaging delays limb-saving treatment
Correct
Masks symptoms and delays definitive treatment
exp: These are classic signs of impending Volkmann's ischemic contracture from compartment syndrome; diagnosis is clinical, and immediate cast removal followed by emergency fasciotomy if symptoms persist prevents irreversible muscle/nerve ischemia - a normal distal pulse can persist despite compartment syndrome, so it must not be used to defer treatment.

subject: Surgery
q: A 62-year-old man has painless progressive jaundice and weight loss. CT abdomen shows a 2.5 cm mass in the head of the pancreas with more than 180 degrees of contact with the superior mesenteric vein, without thrombosis or unreconstructable occlusion, and a clear fat plane around the superior mesenteric artery. This tumor is best classified as:
why: Correct
Resectable tumors have no more than 180 degrees venous contact and no contour irregularity, unlike this case
Unresectable disease requires unreconstructable venous involvement or arterial (not venous) encasement beyond 180 degrees, neither present here
No distant metastasis is described here
exp: Extensive (over 180 degrees) but reconstructable venous (SMV/portal vein) involvement, with no arterial encasement, places a pancreatic tumor in the borderline resectable category per NCCN criteria, typically approached with neoadjuvant therapy before considering resection; venous involvement alone, even if extensive, does not make a tumor unresectable as long as it is reconstructable — that distinction hinges on arterial (SMA/celiac/hepatic) involvement.

q: A 45-year-old man has a reducible right groin swelling. After reduction, firm pressure is applied over the deep inguinal ring (midpoint of the inguino-ligamentous line) and he is asked to cough - the swelling reappears despite this occlusion. This finding indicates a:
why: Would be controlled by occlusion of the deep ring, unlike this case
Correct
Presents below the inguinal ligament, not through the inguinal canal
Presents with obturator canal symptoms, not a groin swelling controlled by this test
exp: In the classic occlusion (Zieman's) test, an indirect hernia is controlled by pressure over the deep ring since it passes through it, whereas a direct hernia bulges through the weak posterior wall of Hesselbach's triangle medial to the inferior epigastric vessels and reappears despite occlusion.

subject: Surgery
q: A 50-year-old woman has a slow-growing, painless, mobile swelling anterior to the right ear tragus for 2 years, with normal facial nerve function. FNAC suggests a pleomorphic adenoma confined to the superficial lobe of the parotid gland. The standard surgical treatment is:
opts: Total parotidectomy sacrificing the facial nerve
Incisional biopsy followed by radiotherapy alone
Superficial parotidectomy with facial nerve preservation
why: Associated with unacceptably high recurrence rates
Unnecessary and would cause avoidable facial nerve morbidity, as the nerve is not involved
Radiotherapy is not primary treatment for a benign salivary tumor
Correct
exp: Superficial parotidectomy with careful facial nerve dissection and preservation is the standard operation for a superficial-lobe pleomorphic adenoma; enucleation alone is avoided due to high recurrence from tumor pseudopod extensions and capsule rupture.

subject: Surgery
q: A 68-year-old smoker has hemoptysis and weight loss. CT chest shows a 4 cm right upper lobe mass with ipsilateral hilar (N1) and subcarinal (N2) lymph node involvement, no distant metastases, and no mediastinal invasion. The subcarinal nodal involvement makes this N2, corresponding to stage IIIA disease, for which the most appropriate management approach is:
opts: Multimodality therapy (neoadjuvant chemotherapy/chemoradiation, with surgery considered thereafter)
why: Upfront surgery alone has poor outcomes in bulky N2 disease
Undertreats resectable-potential disease
Correct
Reserved for metastatic/unfit patients, not this potentially curable stage
exp: Stage IIIA non-small cell lung cancer (bulky N2 disease) is generally managed with multimodality treatment - neoadjuvant chemotherapy or chemoradiation, with surgical resection considered afterward in selected responders - rather than surgery or radiotherapy alone.

subject: Surgery
q: A 55-year-old asymptomatic woman is incidentally found to have a 3 cm left adrenal mass on CT (homogeneous, under 10 Hounsfield units) done for an unrelated reason. Complete hormonal workup - plasma metanephrines, overnight dexamethasone suppression test, and aldosterone-renin ratio - is negative. The most appropriate next step is:
opts: Periodic surveillance imaging and repeat hormonal testing
Fine needle aspiration of the mass
why: Correct
Surgery is reserved for functioning tumors, size over 4 cm, or suspicious imaging features, none present here
Adrenal FNA is generally avoided (needle-tract seeding risk, cannot diagnose adrenocortical carcinoma reliably, and pheochromocytoma must be excluded first)
No indication for steroids in a non-functioning mass
exp: A small (under 4 cm), non-functioning adrenal incidentaloma with benign imaging features (homogeneous, low attenuation) is managed conservatively with periodic imaging and repeat hormonal evaluation rather than surgery.

subject: Surgery
q: A 30-year-old man sustains a degloving injury of the dorsum of the foot after a road traffic accident, with exposed extensor tendons and bone and a poorly vascularized wound bed. A split-thickness skin graft is unlikely to survive in this setting. The most appropriate reconstructive option is:
opts: Delayed split-thickness skin graft after a few weeks
Healing by secondary intention with dressings
why: A graft will still fail on exposed bone/tendon regardless of timing without an intervening vascularized bed
Correct
Leaves bone/tendon exposed to desiccation and infection, unacceptable here
Grafts of any thickness will not take on avascular bone/tendon
exp: Skin grafts require a well-vascularized bed (granulation tissue, muscle, paratenon) to take; exposed bare bone/tendon without paratenon needs vascularized tissue coverage, provided by a local or free microvascular flap - the reconstructive ladder principle.

subject: Surgery
q: A 2-month-old infant has rapidly increasing head circumference crossing percentile lines, a tense bulging anterior fontanelle, and sunset sign of the eyes. Cranial ultrasound shows markedly dilated lateral and third ventricles. The definitive management for this condition is:
opts: Observation, as it usually resolves spontaneously
why: Only a temporizing measure, not definitive treatment
Medical therapy is temporary and not curative for structural obstruction
Untreated progressive hydrocephalus causes permanent neurological damage
Correct
exp: Progressive infantile hydrocephalus with signs of raised intracranial pressure requires definitive CSF diversion, most commonly a ventriculoperitoneal shunt (endoscopic third ventriculostomy is an option in select etiologies); medical measures and serial LPs are at best temporizing.

subject: Surgery
q: A 60-year-old man with altered bowel habits and hematochezia undergoes colonoscopy showing a sigmoid mass; biopsy confirms adenocarcinoma invading through the muscularis propria into pericolic fat, with 3 of 15 lymph nodes positive and no distant metastases on staging CT. This corresponds to AJCC Stage III disease, meaning that after surgical resection he should be offered:
opts: Observation alone, as node-positive disease still has excellent prognosis without further therapy
Adjuvant radiotherapy to the abdomen alone
Adjuvant chemotherapy, since node-positive status changes management regardless of T stage
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy only, with no adjuvant treatment needed
why: Node-positive disease has a substantially worse prognosis without adjuvant therapy
Radiotherapy is not standard for colon cancer (unlike rectal cancer)
Correct
Neoadjuvant therapy is not standard for resectable colon cancer; benefit here comes from post-resection adjuvant chemotherapy
exp: Any node-positive (Stage III) colon cancer is an indication for adjuvant chemotherapy (typically an oxaliplatin-based regimen) after curative resection, regardless of the primary tumor's T stage, to reduce recurrence risk.

subject: Surgery
q: A 65-year-old male smoker has painless gross hematuria. Cystoscopy with transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT) shows a papillary lesion; histopathology confirms invasion into the lamina propria but not into the detrusor muscle. This non-muscle-invasive tumor (stage T1) is best managed with:
opts: Intravesical BCG immunotherapy after complete TURBT
why: Correct
Overtreatment for non-muscle-invasive disease
Not standard primary treatment for NMIBC
Systemic chemotherapy is used for muscle-invasive/metastatic disease, not this stage
exp: Non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (Ta/T1/CIS), especially high-risk T1 disease, is managed with complete TURBT followed by intravesical BCG immunotherapy to reduce recurrence and progression; radical cystectomy is reserved for muscle-invasive or BCG-refractory disease.

subject: Surgery
q: A 30-year-old woman with ptosis and fatigable muscle weakness confirmed as myasthenia gravis undergoes CT chest, which shows a well-defined anterior mediastinal mass. The most likely diagnosis and the treatment of choice are:
why: Lymphoma is not classically linked to myasthenia gravis
Correct
Teratomas are not linked to myasthenia and observation would miss a thymoma
A goiter is not linked to myasthenia gravis
exp: Myasthenia gravis with an anterior mediastinal mass strongly suggests thymoma; thymectomy is both diagnostic and therapeutic, often improving myasthenic symptoms in addition to treating the tumor.

subject: Surgery
q: A 58-year-old woman has abdominal distension and an adnexal mass on ultrasound, with a markedly elevated serum CA-125. In epithelial ovarian cancer, CA-125 is clinically most useful for:
opts: Population-based screening in asymptomatic women, given its high specificity
Confirming the tissue diagnosis without a biopsy
Determining the histological subtype of the tumor
Monitoring response to treatment and detecting recurrence, though it lacks specificity for diagnosis
why: Poor specificity makes it unsuitable for population screening
Tissue diagnosis still requires histopathology
It does not distinguish histological subtypes
Correct
exp: CA-125 is useful for monitoring treatment response and detecting recurrence in known epithelial ovarian cancer, but performs poorly as a population screening test because it is also elevated in many benign conditions (endometriosis, fibroids, pelvic infection, pregnancy, menstruation).
