q: A 55-year-old man is evaluated for painless, progressive jaundice, weight loss, and a palpable, non-tender, distended gallbladder on examination. Which statement best supports the conclusion that gallstone disease is an unlikely cause, per Courvoisier's law?
opts: Gallstones typically cause intermittent, not progressive, obstruction of the bile duct
Long-standing calculous disease fibroses and shrinks the gallbladder wall, so it cannot distend even when the CBD is obstructed downstream
The gallbladder is intrahepatic and therefore impalpable in cholelithiasis
Painless jaundice excludes any biliary tract stone disease by definition
why: Wrong — intermittency isn't the basis of the law; the fibrotic, non-distensible wall is.
Correct — chronic stone disease scars the gallbladder so it cannot distend under pressure.
Wrong — the gallbladder is extrahepatic and would be palpable if it did distend; that's not why it doesn't.
Wrong — painless jaundice is suggestive but not absolute; the law's logic is wall fibrosis, not pain.
exp: Courvoisier's law: in a jaundiced patient, a palpable non-tender gallbladder suggests malignant obstruction (periampullary carcinoma, cholangiocarcinoma, carcinoma of the pancreatic head) rather than gallstones, because chronic calculous cholecystitis fibroses and shrinks the gallbladder, preventing it from distending even under pressure. Exceptions exist (Mirizzi syndrome, double impaction).

subject: Surgery
q: A 70-year-old woman presents with a rapidly enlarging, hard, fixed neck mass over 4 weeks, with hoarseness, dysphagia, and stridor, arising in the setting of a longstanding multinodular goitre. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Correct — rapid growth over weeks with invasive features (hoarseness, dysphagia, stridor) in an elderly patient with a prior goitre is classic anaplastic carcinoma.
Wrong — papillary carcinoma grows slowly over years and rarely causes this rapid, aggressive local invasion.
Wrong — Riedel's thyroiditis produces a woody-hard gland from fibrosis but progresses over months to years, and is not a malignancy.
Wrong — thyroid lymphoma can also grow rapidly but classically arises against a background of Hashimoto's thyroiditis and is far rarer; anaplastic carcinoma is the more classic answer here.
exp: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma is one of the most aggressive human malignancies — rapid growth over weeks, with local invasion causing hoarseness (recurrent laryngeal nerve), dysphagia, and stridor (tracheal compression), typically in elderly patients, often against a background of a longstanding goitre or pre-existing well-differentiated thyroid cancer. Prognosis is dismal; management is largely palliative since curative surgery is rarely possible.

subject: Surgery
q: A 40-year-old man presents with recurrent peptic ulcers refractory to therapy, renal stones from hypercalcemia, and a pituitary mass causing headaches and visual field defects. Which syndrome links these three findings?
why: Wrong — MEN2A involves medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma, not pituitary tumours or refractory peptic ulcer disease.
Correct — the 3 P's (parathyroid, pancreatic/gastrinoma causing refractory ulcers, pituitary) define MEN1.
Wrong — MEN2B involves medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and mucosal neuromas, with no pituitary or gastrinoma component.
Wrong — VHL causes hemangioblastomas, renal cell carcinoma, and pheochromocytoma, not this triad.
exp: MEN1 (Wermer syndrome, MEN1 gene/menin mutation, autosomal dominant) presents with the classic triad of parathyroid hyperplasia/adenoma (hypercalcemia, renal stones), pancreatic islet cell tumours (gastrinoma causing refractory Zollinger-Ellison-type ulcers, or insulinoma), and pituitary adenoma (most commonly prolactinoma) — mnemonic the 3 P's. Distinct from MEN2A and MEN2B, both RET mutations.

subject: Surgery
q: A 72-year-old with atrial fibrillation presents with sudden severe abdominal pain out of proportion to a benign abdominal exam, followed by bloody diarrhoea. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
opts: Acute mesenteric ischemia due to embolism
why: Wrong — pancreatitis causes epigastric pain typically proportional to exam tenderness, not this classic pain-out-of-proportion pattern.
Wrong — a perforated ulcer causes sudden severe pain WITH peritonitis from the outset, not an initially benign exam.
Correct — pain out of proportion in an AF patient, progressing to bloody diarrhoea, is classic embolic mesenteric ischemia.
Wrong — diverticulitis causes localized left iliac fossa pain proportional to exam findings, not this AF-related embolic pattern.
exp: Acute mesenteric ischemia classically presents with pain out of proportion to exam findings early on, often in a patient with atrial fibrillation, since the embolic source typically lodges in the SMA just past the origin of the middle colic artery. Later features include bloody diarrhoea, progressing to peritonitis as transmural infarction occurs. Mortality is high; management needs urgent CT angiography and surgical exploration.

q: A 62-year-old diabetic smoker presents with intermittent claudication of the right calf occurring after walking about 100 metres. Doppler evaluation reveals an ankle-brachial index of 0.65, with normal femoral and popliteal pulses proximally. Which of the following best describes his disease severity and the most appropriate initial management?
opts: Mild-to-moderate peripheral arterial disease (ABI 0.5 to 0.9) — optimise risk factors, supervised exercise therapy, and antiplatelet agents
Critical limb ischaemia (ABI less than 0.4) — needs urgent surgical revascularisation
Normal ABI — peripheral arterial disease is excluded
Non-compressible calcified vessel (ABI greater than 1.3) — proceed to toe-brachial index
why: Correct — ABI 0.65 is mild-to-moderate PAD managed conservatively, not surgically.
Critical ischaemia requiring urgent revascularisation corresponds to ABI less than 0.4, not 0.65.
0.65 is abnormal, so PAD is present, not excluded.
ABI greater than 1.3, non-compressible vessels, does not match this patient's measured 0.65.
exp: ABI grades PAD severity: greater than 1.3 suggests non-compressible calcified vessels; 0.9 to 1.3 is normal; 0.5 to 0.9 correlates with mild-to-moderate disease and claudication, managed conservatively with supervised exercise, smoking cessation, statin, antiplatelet therapy, and glycaemic control before considering revascularisation; less than 0.4 signifies critical ischaemia often needing urgent intervention.

subject: Surgery
q: A 45-year-old man develops sudden severe retrosternal chest pain and breathlessness immediately after an episode of forceful, repeated vomiting following a heavy alcohol binge. On examination there is subcutaneous crepitus over the neck and chest, and a crunching sound synchronous with the heartbeat is heard on auscultation. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
why: MI does not produce subcutaneous emphysema or a mediastinal crunch
Mallory-Weiss tear is a mucosal-only tear causing hematemesis, not full-thickness rupture with crepitus
Pneumothorax alone does not classically produce a crunch synchronous with the heartbeat
Correct — forceful vomiting plus crepitus plus Hamman's crunch is Boerhaave syndrome
exp: Boerhaave syndrome is a full-thickness esophageal rupture caused by a sudden rise in intraluminal pressure against a closed glottis during forceful retching; the mediastinal crunch (Hamman's sign) and subcutaneous emphysema are classic clues, and mortality rises steeply if contrast esophagography/CT and surgical repair are delayed beyond 24 hours.

subject: Surgery
q: A 35-year-old woman presents with a solitary, firm, non-tender thyroid nodule. Thyroid function tests are normal. FNAC is reported as follicular neoplasm (Bethesda category IV). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Start levothyroxine suppression therapy and reassess in 3 months
why: Repeat FNAC will not resolve the adenoma-vs-carcinoma question, which needs capsular/vascular architecture
Suppression therapy delays a tissue diagnosis and has no proven benefit in a Bethesda IV nodule
Total thyroidectomy up front is premature before histology confirms malignancy
correct — diagnostic lobectomy provides the tissue needed to assess invasion
exp: FNAC cytology cannot distinguish a follicular adenoma from a follicular carcinoma — that distinction depends entirely on capsular and/or vascular invasion, seen only on histopathology of the excised lobe. A follicular-neoplasm FNAC report always mandates diagnostic lobectomy; completion thyroidectomy is reserved for cases where histopathology confirms malignancy.

subject: Surgery
q: A 28-year-old male heavy smoker presents with intermittent claudication of the foot, migratory superficial thrombophlebitis, and a non-healing ulcer on the great toe. Lipid profile is normal and there is no history of diabetes. Angiography shows segmental occlusive lesions of distal small and medium vessels with characteristic corkscrew collaterals. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line management?
opts: Complete and absolute cessation of tobacco use
why: Statins target atherosclerotic lipid-driven disease, irrelevant here given a normal lipid profile and non-atherosclerotic pathology
correct — smoking cessation is the only proven disease-modifying intervention in Buerger's disease
Anticoagulation has no proven role in altering the disease course
Distal small-vessel involvement usually makes vessels unsuitable for bypass; reserved for select cases after cessation fails
exp: This is thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger's disease) — a segmental, non-atherosclerotic inflammatory vasculitis of small and medium vessels in young smokers, marked by migratory superficial thrombophlebitis and corkscrew collaterals on angiography, with a normal lipid profile distinguishing it from atherosclerotic peripheral arterial disease. Complete tobacco cessation is the only intervention proven to halt progression and prevent amputation.

subject: Surgery
q: A 22-year-old man presents with periumbilical pain migrating to the right iliac fossa over 18 hours, associated with anorexia, low-grade fever, and localized tenderness at McBurney's point with rebound tenderness. His Alvarado score is calculated at 8. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Discharge with oral antibiotics and outpatient follow-up
Observe for 48 hours with serial abdominal examinations only
Proceed to appendectomy without further imaging
Perform a barium enema to confirm the diagnosis
why: Wrong — discharging a high-probability surgical abdomen risks perforation and peritonitis.
Wrong — prolonged observation in a high Alvarado score risks progression to perforation.
Correct — an Alvarado score of 7-10 supports proceeding directly to appendectomy in a classic presentation.
Wrong — barium enema is not used to diagnose appendicitis and risks perforation.
exp: An Alvarado score of 7-10 in a classic clinical picture of appendicitis supports proceeding directly to appendectomy without further imaging; scores of 5-6 are equivocal and warrant USG/CT, while scores below 5 make appendicitis unlikely.

q: A 45-year-old man presents with progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids over 8 months, regurgitation of undigested food, and significant weight loss. Barium swallow shows a dilated esophagus with smooth tapering at the lower end giving a bird-beak appearance. Which investigation should be done next to confirm the diagnosis before planning treatment?
why: Endoscopy is mandatory beforehand to exclude a mimicking malignancy (pseudoachalasia) but does not by itself confirm the motility diagnosis.
CT chest is used for staging or to exclude pseudoachalasia from a mediastinal/GE-junction tumour, not to confirm achalasia itself.
pH monitoring diagnoses gastro-esophageal reflux disease, which does not explain dysphagia to solids and liquids together.
Correct — manometry is the gold standard, demonstrating esophageal aperistalsis and failure of lower esophageal sphincter relaxation, confirming achalasia cardia.
exp: Achalasia cardia should be suspected when dysphagia involves both solids and liquids (a motility disorder, unlike a mechanical stricture that affects solids first) with a bird-beak sign on barium swallow. Esophageal manometry is the gold-standard confirmatory test (aperistalsis + incomplete LES relaxation), though endoscopy is still mandatory beforehand to rule out pseudoachalasia from a distal esophageal or cardia malignancy.

subject: Surgery
q: A 6-year-old girl presents with intermittent right upper quadrant pain, jaundice, and a palpable abdominal mass; ultrasound shows fusiform dilatation of the extrahepatic common bile duct with normal-calibre intrahepatic ducts. The definitive management to prevent long-term malignant transformation is:
opts: Complete cyst excision with Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy
why: Percutaneous drainage leaves the at-risk cyst epithelium behind and the cyst recurs
Sphincterotomy/stenting is used for stone extraction, not choledochal cyst treatment
Correct — complete excision removes the malignancy-prone epithelium entirely
Internal cyst-enterostomy is an older, now-abandoned technique leaving cyst mucosa in situ with ongoing cancer risk
exp: This is a classic Type I choledochal cyst (the pain-jaundice-mass triad is textbook-classic though present in only a minority); standard of care is complete cyst excision with Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy, because retained cyst epithelium carries a lifelong cholangiocarcinoma risk.

subject: Surgery
q: A 25-year-old man presents with a right scrotal swelling for 3 months, painless and gradually increasing in size. On examination the swelling is cystic, brilliantly transilluminant, the examiner can "get above" the swelling on bimanual palpation, and the testis cannot be felt separately from it. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Correct — cystic, transilluminant, "get above" it, testis impalpable separately: classic vaginal hydrocele.
An inguinal hernia is continuous with the inguinal canal, so the examiner cannot get above it, and it is reducible/gives a cough impulse.
An epididymal cyst is separate from and posterior to the testis, often multilocular, and the testis is palpable separately from it.
A varicocele feels like a "bag of worms," is not transilluminant, and characteristically empties/reduces on lying supine.
exp: Vaginal hydrocele is a cystic collection of fluid within the tunica vaginalis, lying below and anterior to the testis. It is brilliantly transilluminant, and — unlike an inguinal hernia — the examiner can "get above" it. The testis lies within the sac and so cannot be palpated separately, distinguishing it from an epididymal cyst.

subject: Surgery
q: A 68-year-old man with atrial fibrillation, not on anticoagulation, develops sudden severe pain, pallor, and coldness of the right leg over the past 2 hours. The limb is pulseless below the femoral artery, with reduced sensation and mild weakness of the foot. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
opts: Immediate IV heparin anticoagulation and urgent embolectomy
Start oral aspirin and observe for 24 hours
Duplex ultrasound of the leg veins to rule out DVT first
why: Correct — anticoagulate immediately and proceed to urgent revascularization
Oral aspirin alone and 24-hour observation would allow irreversible muscle/nerve necrosis in a limb already showing sensory and motor deficit
Duplex venous imaging investigates DVT, not arterial occlusion, and delays definitive treatment
Elective imaging and elective angioplasty are far too slow for a limb with neurological deficit
exp: This is acute limb ischaemia from cardioembolic occlusion (source: AF) - pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, and now paralysis are the classic 6 P's progression signalling a limb-threatening, time-critical emergency. Immediate systemic heparinization plus urgent embolectomy (Fogarty catheter) or thrombolysis is required within hours to salvage the limb.

q: A child sustains a circumferential full-thickness flame burn of the right forearm. Six hours later the hand is cold with absent capillary refill and a diminishing radial pulse on Doppler, despite adequate Parkland fluid resuscitation. What is the most appropriate immediate step?
opts: Increase the rate of intravenous fluids
why: Correct - escharotomy releases the constricting non-viable eschar and is the immediate limb-saving step
More fluid does not relieve mechanical compression from the rigid eschar and will not restore distal perfusion
Fasciotomy is indicated for true compartment syndrome beneath intact fascia, not the first step for eschar-related constriction
Skin grafting is a later reconstructive step performed once the wound is stable, not an emergency perfusion-saving measure
exp: A circumferential full-thickness (eschar) burn forms an inelastic, tourniquet-like band; as underlying tissue edema develops it compresses vessels and nerves, causing limb-threatening ischemia irrespective of fluid status. Escharotomy - a longitudinal incision through the non-viable eschar down to healthy subcutaneous tissue (not through deep fascia) - releases the constriction and is the immediate limb-saving step.

subject: Surgery
q: A 32-year-old woman presents with a painless solitary thyroid nodule. FNAC shows cells with overlapping nuclei, finely dispersed ground-glass chromatin (Orphan Annie eye nuclei), intranuclear cytoplasmic pseudoinclusions, and psammoma bodies. Which statement about this condition is correct?
opts: It behaves aggressively once lymph node metastasis occurs, which markedly worsens prognosis
It is the most common thyroid malignancy, spreads primarily via lymphatics, and carries an excellent overall prognosis even with nodal disease
It arises from parafollicular C cells and secretes calcitonin
It typically presents with early hematogenous spread to bone and lungs, with lymphatic spread being rare
why: Incorrect — nodal spread in papillary carcinoma does not carry the same ominous prognostic weight it does in most other cancers
Correct
This describes medullary thyroid carcinoma, not papillary — different cytology (amyloid stroma, calcitonin)
Papillary carcinoma spreads mainly via lymphatics; early hematogenous spread is more typical of follicular carcinoma
exp: Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the commonest thyroid cancer; the cytology described (Orphan Annie eye nuclei, nuclear grooves/pseudoinclusions, psammoma bodies) is classic for it. It spreads predominantly via lymphatics to cervical nodes, and unlike most solid cancers, nodal metastasis does not significantly worsen prognosis in patients under about 55 — overall 10-year survival remains excellent.

subject: Surgery
q: A 55-year-old woman with a long history of gallstones presents with painless, progressive jaundice and pruritus. Ultrasound shows a stone impacted in the gallbladder neck/cystic duct causing extrinsic compression and narrowing of the common hepatic duct, with dilated intrahepatic ducts above the obstruction and a normal-calibre common bile duct below it. There is no mass lesion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Mirizzi syndrome — extrinsic common hepatic duct compression by an impacted cystic duct/gallbladder-neck stone
Choledocholithiasis with a stone in the common bile duct
why: Correct
A Klatskin tumour is a mass lesion at the hilum, not extrinsic compression from an impacted stone
Choledocholithiasis shows an intraluminal stone within the dilated CBD itself, not extrinsic compression from the cystic duct
Courvoisier's law refers to a palpable non-tender gallbladder from distal CBD obstruction (usually periampullary/pancreatic head malignancy), not the mechanism described here
exp: Mirizzi syndrome results from a gallstone impacted in the cystic duct or gallbladder neck causing extrinsic compression of the adjacent common hepatic duct, producing obstructive jaundice that mimics a hilar malignancy; the key clue is dilated ducts above an extrinsic (not intraluminal or mass) narrowing in a patient with chronic cholelithiasis. MRCP/ERCP confirms it, and recognising it before surgery is essential to avoid bile duct injury.

subject: Surgery
q: Six hours after a free DIEP flap breast reconstruction, the flap is swollen and dusky blue, with brisk dark blood on pinprick testing and rapid capillary refill (less than 1 second). What is the most likely cause?
opts: Flap desiccation from an inadequate dressing
why: Arterial thrombosis produces a pale, cool flap with no pinprick bleeding, not congestion
Correct — dusky, blue, swollen with brisk dark bleeding is textbook venous congestion
Desiccation would show a dry, cool, non-bleeding flap, not this picture
This appearance is never normal and mandates urgent surgical reassessment
exp: A congested, dusky-blue, swollen flap with brisk dark bleeding on pinprick and fast capillary refill is the classic picture of venous congestion — the mirror image of arterial insufficiency (pale, cool, no bleeding, slow refill) — and demands urgent re-exploration to salvage venous drainage.

subject: Surgery
q: A 52-year-old woman on routine health screening is found to have serum calcium 11.8 mg/dL (upper normal 10.2), elevated intact PTH, and low serum phosphate. She has no symptoms. Sestamibi scan localizes a single right inferior parathyroid adenoma, and bone density shows no osteoporosis. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
opts: Lifelong observation with annual serum calcium monitoring
why: Observation is reserved for patients not meeting surgical criteria; this patient's calcium exceeds the accepted threshold above the upper limit of normal
Correct — a single localized adenoma in a patient meeting surgical criteria is treated with focused minimally invasive parathyroidectomy with intraoperative PTH monitoring
Cinacalcet is used for poor surgical candidates or parathyroid carcinoma with hypercalcemia, not first-line for a localized single adenoma
Total parathyroidectomy with autotransplantation is reserved for multiglandular disease such as MEN-associated hyperplasia, not a single adenoma
exp: Surgery is indicated in primary hyperparathyroidism even if asymptomatic when serum calcium is well above the upper limit of normal, among other criteria (low bone density, reduced renal function, younger age). A single localized adenoma on sestamibi is treated with minimally invasive parathyroidectomy with intraoperative PTH monitoring to confirm cure.

subject: Surgery
q: A 30-year-old man has a large raw granulating wound on the anterior thigh following debridement of a burn injury. The surgeon plans reconstruction using a dermatome-harvested graft containing epidermis plus a variable portion of dermis, which has better graft take but more secondary contracture than the alternative graft type. What type of graft is being described?
why: Full-thickness grafts include the entire dermis - better cosmesis, less contracture, but poorer graft take - the opposite trade-off described here
Correct - split-thickness graft, dermatome-harvested, better take with more contracture
Composite grafts include skin plus underlying structures like cartilage, not relevant here
A free vascularized flap brings its own blood supply via microvascular anastomosis, unlike an avascular graft
exp: Split-thickness skin grafts (STSG) contain epidermis plus a variable portion of dermis, harvested with a dermatome; they have better graft take but greater secondary contracture than full-thickness grafts (FTSG), which include the entire dermis, give better cosmesis and durability, but need a well-vascularized recipient bed.

subject: Surgery
q: A 68-year-old man with a known history of hypertension and long-standing smoking presents to the emergency department with sudden severe abdominal and back pain, hypotension, and a pulsatile abdominal mass on examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Acute pancreatitis causes epigastric pain radiating to the back but not typically a pulsatile mass with this hypotension pattern
Perforated peptic ulcer causes sudden severe abdominal pain with peritonitis, not a pulsatile mass
Correct - classic triad of pain, hypotension, and pulsatile mass in a smoker with hypertension
Renal colic causes colicky flank pain radiating to the groin, not hypotension or a pulsatile mass
exp: The classic triad of ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm is sudden severe abdominal/back pain, hypotension, and a pulsatile abdominal mass, though the complete triad is present in only about 50% of cases. It is a surgical emergency requiring immediate resuscitation and repair; major risk factors include smoking, hypertension, atherosclerosis, and age over 65.

subject: Surgery
q: A 45-year-old man presents 2 days after a road traffic accident with chest trauma, now with hypotension, distended neck veins, and muffled heart sounds. On examination, systolic BP falls by 15 mmHg during inspiration. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Correct - Beck's triad plus pulsus paradoxus is diagnostic of tamponade
Tension pneumothorax presents with tracheal deviation, hyperresonance, and absent breath sounds, not muffled heart sounds
Massive hemothorax causes dullness to percussion and hypovolemic shock, not JVD or muffled heart sounds
Flail chest presents with paradoxical chest wall movement on inspection, not Beck's triad
exp: Beck's triad (hypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds) plus pulsus paradoxus (inspiratory SBP fall greater than 10 mmHg) is classic for cardiac tamponade from traumatic hemopericardium; management is emergency pericardiocentesis or pericardial window, not needle decompression.

subject: Surgery
q: A 22-year-old woman presents 8 months after ear piercing with a firm, itchy, raised scar that has grown beyond the piercing site onto adjacent normal skin and shows no sign of regression. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment for this keloid?
why: Correct - intralesional triamcinolone is first-line therapy for keloids, reducing collagen synthesis and inflammation.
Surgical excision alone carries a high recurrence rate (up to 50-80 percent) unless combined with adjuvant therapy.
Systemic oral steroids are not the standard approach for a localized keloid.
Keloids are not infective; topical antibiotics have no role in their management.
exp: Keloids differ from hypertrophic scars by extending beyond the original wound margins into normal skin, continuing to grow after 6 months, and rarely regressing spontaneously. First-line treatment is intralesional corticosteroid (triamcinolone acetonide) injection, often combined with silicone gel sheeting or pressure therapy; excision alone has a high recurrence rate and should be combined with adjuvant therapy.

subject: Surgery
q: A 55-year-old woman who underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy two years ago presents with high-grade fever with chills, right upper quadrant pain, jaundice, and now confusion with hypotension. What is the most likely diagnosis and the most appropriate next step?
opts: Acute cholecystitis; start IV antibiotics and plan interval cholecystectomy
Acute pancreatitis; keep nil by mouth and give IV fluids
why: Acute cholecystitis does not typically cause jaundice or Reynolds' pentad, and this patient's gallbladder is already removed
Observation alone is inadequate for a patient in sepsis with biliary obstruction
Correct - this is Reynolds' pentad of suppurative cholangitis needing emergent decompression
Pancreatitis does not classically present with this fever-jaundice-shock pentad from biliary obstruction
exp: Fever with chills plus jaundice plus RUQ pain (Charcot's triad), now with altered mentation and hypotension added (Reynolds' pentad), indicates severe suppurative ascending cholangitis - a surgical emergency needing IV antibiotics AND urgent biliary decompression, most commonly ERCP with sphincterotomy/stenting after initial resuscitation; delay risks septic shock and death.

subject: Surgery
q: A 45-year-old man presents with a firm thyroid nodule. His father died of a pheochromocytoma and his sister has primary hyperparathyroidism. FNAC of the nodule shows amyloid-containing stroma, and serum calcitonin is markedly elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Papillary carcinoma shows psammoma bodies and Orphan Annie-eye nuclei, not calcitonin secretion
Follicular carcinoma spreads hematogenously via capsular/vascular invasion, unrelated to amyloid stroma or calcitonin
Anaplastic carcinoma occurs in elderly patients as a rapidly growing aggressive mass, with no MEN association
Correct — amyloid stroma, elevated calcitonin, and family history of pheochromocytoma plus hyperparathyroidism indicate medullary thyroid carcinoma as part of MEN 2A
exp: Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells, secretes calcitonin (used as a tumor marker and for postoperative surveillance), and shows characteristic amyloid deposition in the stroma on histology. Around 25% are familial, occurring as part of MEN 2A (MTC plus pheochromocytoma plus primary hyperparathyroidism) or MEN 2B (MTC plus pheochromocytoma plus mucosal neuromas/marfanoid habitus) due to RET proto-oncogene mutations — screen family members with RET testing and consider prophylactic thyroidectomy in gene carriers.

subject: Surgery
q: Twelve hours after a free fibular flap for mandibular reconstruction, the flap skin paddle becomes pale, cool, and capillary refill is markedly slowed beyond 5 seconds with no bleeding on pinprick testing; pulses were normal at the end of surgery. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Venous congestion — release a tight dressing and consider leech therapy
Normal post-operative flap physiology — continue routine observation
Arterial insufficiency — urgent surgical re-exploration is indicated
Flap infection — start broad-spectrum antibiotics and observe
why: Venous congestion gives the opposite picture — swollen, dusky-blue, warm flap with brisk dark bleeding on pinprick
Pallor with absent capillary refill is never normal flap physiology and signals impending flap loss
Correct — pale, cool, no bleeding on pinprick is the bedside signature of arterial insufficiency requiring emergency re-exploration
Infection presents later, over days, with erythema, warmth, and purulent discharge, not acute pallor at 12 hours
exp: Pallor, coolness, and delayed or absent capillary refill with no bleeding on pinprick point to arterial insufficiency, as opposed to venous congestion (dusky, swollen, warm, brisk dark bleeding); flap salvage is time-critical, so this picture mandates emergency re-exploration.

subject: Surgery
q: A 70-year-old bedridden man on antipsychotic medication is brought in with three days of progressive abdominal distension and absolute constipation; supine abdominal X-ray shows a grossly dilated loop with a coffee-bean appearance and no signs of peritonism or gangrene. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
opts: Rigid/flexible sigmoidoscopic decompression with flatus tube insertion
Barium enema as the first-line diagnostic and therapeutic step
Conservative management with nasogastric decompression and IV fluids alone
why: Emergency laparotomy is reserved for peritonitis, gangrene, perforation, or failed endoscopic detorsion, not first-line here.
Correct — endoscopic (sigmoidoscopic) decompression with a flatus tube relieves obstruction in viable volvulus, allowing elective resection later to prevent recurrence.
Barium enema can show a bird's-beak deformity but is not the therapeutic step of choice and risks perforation in a distended obstructed colon.
Conservative NG decompression alone does not relieve a closed-loop volvulus and risks progression to ischemia.
exp: Sigmoid volvulus (elderly, chronic constipation, psychiatric drugs/nursing home risk factors) shows a coffee-bean or bent-inner-tube sign on erect/supine X-ray. In a stable patient without peritonism, endoscopic (sigmoidoscopic) detorsion and flatus tube decompression is first-line, followed by elective sigmoid resection to prevent recurrence (recurrence rate is high without surgery). Peritonism, gangrene, or failed endoscopic reduction mandates emergency laparotomy.

subject: Surgery
q: A 32-year-old mechanic sustains a crush avulsion injury to the dorsum of his right hand at work, with a 6x4 cm area of skin loss exposing the extensor tendons and underlying bone. Which of the following is the most appropriate reconstructive option?
opts: Vascularized flap cover (e.g., groin flap or radial forearm flap)
Healing by secondary intention with regular dressings
why: Fails on avascular exposed tendon/bone — needs a vascular bed to take
Also needs a vascularized bed and is reserved for smaller, cosmetically sensitive defects, not exposed tendon
Correct — a pedicled or free flap brings its own blood supply and can safely cover exposed tendon/bone
Secondary intention over exposed tendon risks desiccation, infection, and tendon necrosis/adhesion
exp: Skin grafts (split- or full-thickness) depend on a vascularized recipient bed for take by imbibition and inosculation; exposed avascular structures like bare tendon, bone, or cartilage cannot support a graft and need vascularized flap cover instead. This split-thickness-vs-flap distinction, built on the reconstructive ladder, is a classic NEET PG plastic surgery question.
